title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 5 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - DECEMBER 02: Steve Smith #89 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates after a catch during their game against the San Francisco 49ers at Bank of America Stadium on December 2, 2007 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Streeter Lecka/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #5. Steve Smith, Sr Throughout the history of sports, there have been many players who play with a chip on their shoulder. This skill of turning extrinsic motivation intrinsic has allowed countless players to go beyond their limits and dominate their opponents. Steve Smith might have had the largest chip ever. Standing at just 5’9” and weighing under 200 pounds, Smith was overlooked by major college programs. He started his collegiate career at Santa Monica College before transferring to Utah for his junior campaign. Smith immediately made an impact, especially on special teams, scoring 11 total touchdowns including an NCAA high three punt return touchdowns. His senior season in 2000 was not as spectacular, but he still averaged over 20 yards per reception. The lack of definitive improvement from his junior season to his senior year led to him dropping down draft boards, which turned out to be incredibly lucky for the Carolina Panthers. In the 2001 NFL Draft, the Panthers took Dan Morgan in the first round, Kris Jenkins in the second, and finally took Smith in the third round. Despite major pundits like The Sporting News declaring that the team wasted a third round pick on a guy who would just be a punt returner, Smith became a dominant force on the offense just as the other two became dominant pieces for Carolina’s defense. The pundits weren’t wrong about Smith’s impact on special teams, either. On his first career touch, Smith took the opening kickoff of the 2001 season against the Minnesota Vikings 93 yards for a touchdown, one of three return touchdowns his rookie year (two kickoff returns, one punt return). Smith ended up being one of the few bright spots in that doomed 2001 season, earning Pro Bowl and First Team All Pro honors as a returner. The 2002 season showed flashes of what would come from the wide receiver Steve Smith. Paired up with Muhsin Muhammad, the duo put up some decent stats despite less than stellar quarterback play. As was the case for most Panthers, it was 2003 that really shone a spotlight on Smith’s talent. He exploded onto the scene with 88 catches for 1,110 yards and seven touchdowns, adding another punt return touchdown for good measure. His impact went beyond the box score, however, as he became new quarterback Jake Delhomme’s favorite target. The unforgettable Super Bowl run was largely driven by a dominant defense, but Smith provided the offensive fireworks necessary for the team to advance. His 32 yard touchdown catch in the third quarter of the Wild Card game against the Dallas Cowboys all but sealed the win for the Panthers, his now infamous 69 yard “X-Clown” touchdown reception in double overtime against the Rams pushed the team into the NFC Championship Game, and he added a game-tying 39 yard touchdown in the second quarter of the Super Bowl. While the Panthers would not see team success of that nature for another dozen years, Smith blossomed into one of the best wide receivers in the NFL. Despite breaking his leg in the first game of the 2004 season, he returned at full strength in 2005, winning the receiving triple crown (though only tied for first in receiving touchdowns). His line of 103 catches for 1.563 yards and 12 touchdowns were video game numbers. Those 103 catches would be Panthers single season records until some guy named Christian McCaffrey came along seven years later, and the 1,563 receiving yards is still a Panthers record. For the second time in his five year career, Smith was named to the Pro Bowl and First Team All Pro roster while also taking home the Comeback Player of the Year Award. He would go on to make three more Pro Bowls (2006, 2008, and 2011) and a Second Team All Pro nod in 2008. With the arrival of new Face of the Franchise Cam Newton, Smith struggled to take on more of a secondary role. While his production was still bordering on elite until 2013, there was always an undercurrent of strife between him and Cam. That sense of locker room distraction combined with the Panthers wanting to get younger and cheaper at the position led to the team releasing Smith in March of 2014. Two days later, he signed with the Baltimore Ravens. He would end up playing three years with the Ravens, even eclipsing the thousand yard mark in 2014. Smith’s contract with the Ravens expired in 2017, and a lack of interest from other teams led to his retirement. Steve Smith’s legacy in Carolina goes well beyond stats, though he holds some incredible receiving marks in Panthers history: he’s the all-time Panthers leader in targets (1,438), catches (836), yards (12,197), touchdowns (67), and yards per game (67). He also leads the team in punt returns (178), punt return yards (1,652), punt return touchdowns (4), and longest punt return (87 yards), while finishing second only to Michael Bates in kickoff returns (98), kickoff return yards (2,371), and kickoff return touchdowns (2). Smith finished his career in the top ten in NFL history in all-purpose yards and should be a Hall of Famer at some point. But it’s not the numbers that matter to Panthers fans, it’s the moments: X-Clown, the 2006 playoff game against the Bears, the sideline quotes, the touchdown celebrations, breaking his arm and still scoring a touchdown against the Giants in 2009, grabbing Malcom Jenkins and dragging him by the facemask after scoring a touchdown against the Saints in 2011, and even (unfortunately) the “blood and guts” game against the Panthers in 2014. Despite all the numbers he racked up on the field, the only number that matters at the end of the day to Panthers fans? 89. Bottom line.

title: Panthers fans unmoved by 3-1 preseason record
summary: The Carolina Panthers have had two big problems in their first two seasons under head coach Dave Canales. They have had notoriously slow starts and remarkably shallow rosters. The roster was largely an inherited problem, attributable largely to a decade of poor drafting. In a way, that has also led to the poor starts as […]
full_text: CANTON, OHIO - AUGUST 06: Haynes King #16 of the Carolina Panthers scores a five-yard touchdown to defeat the Arizona Cardinals 33-30 in the 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame Game at Tom Benson Hall Of Fame Stadium on August 06, 2026 in Canton, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers have had two big problems in their first two seasons under head coach Dave Canales. They have had notoriously slow starts and remarkably shallow rosters. The roster was largely an inherited problem, attributable largely to a decade of poor drafting. In a way, that has also led to the poor starts as one has to imagine the coaches spending all of their energy trying to field a competitive team with athletes that wouldn’t have made their way onto another roster. The 3-1 start from this preseason is a sign that things may be changing. Sure, the starters still looked a few gears behind in the race compared to the competition, but the depth was finally at least equal to—and often better—than their counterparts on the other sideline. That led us to ask y’all last week if you felt better, the same, or worse about the 2026 Carolina Panthers after watching them find success in the preseason. As it turns out, most of y’all have seen too many flashes in the pan and ultimately false promises to believe anything from this team before they have shown who they are in the regular season. That’s fair. The Panthers have not been a team to reward faith for a long, long time. It is an honest, sad sign of how far we’ve come that a majority of fans didn’t find a way to look at this relatively successful preseason and feel worse about the team. I’ll leave you with this one thought. This is the best roster that Canales has fielded in his going on three seasons. He has improved each year thus far. The relative health and quality of some of the starters still implies, to me, a slow start to the season. The hope for this year lies in a stronger finish thanks to increased quality in the depth and the fact that Canales’ teams have tended to get better towards the end of the season. Last season, the Panthers needed one extra win against either the Tampa Bay Buccaneers or the New Orleans Saints, both teams with losing records, in the last four weeks of the 2025 season to clinch their first playoff trip in a decade. Instead, they ran out of gas and limped into the postseason (hooray, and such) with a losing record and a giant, divisional asterisk. They put on a good show against the Los Angeles Rams, against whom they apparently match up well, but they were clearly overmatched and outgunned down the stretch. title: The Optimist: Taxing depth early as a sign of progress
summary: The Carolina Panthers are entering the 2026 season in a weird place. On the surface, the wheels are falling off before the bus has even left the station. Their two starting offensive tackles, Taylor Moton and Ikem Ekwonu, are on various reserve lists, along with starting defensive tackle Tershawn Wharton, and all are expected to […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Monroe Freeling #57 of the Carolina Panthers waits for the snap against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers are entering the 2026 season in a weird place. On the surface, the wheels are falling off before the bus has even left the station. Their two starting offensive tackles, Taylor Moton and Ikem Ekwonu, are on various reserve lists, along with starting defensive tackle Tershawn Wharton, and all are expected to miss the first four to six weeks. Their favorite play-all-five-spots utility lineman, Brady Christiansen is out for at least another month recovering from an injury suffered last season. Nic Scourton, a projected starting outside linebacker coming off a breakout rookie season, is out for the season. So too is their third round pick, wide receiver and human highlight reel Chris Brazzell II. They were so disappointed with the middle of the defense during the preseason that they found a free agent linebacker who stayed home during the whole offseason in Bobby Okereke and signed him into a starting role. In short, the offensive line never even got assembled before it started falling apart and the defense is shaky and untested at best. So why aren’t we all freaking out? Why are a lot of us looking around the division and thinking “we might be able to repeat”? Simply put, this is the deepest roster the Carolina Panthers have fielded in years. Injuries happen every year to every team. Depth, as often as anything, separates the teams that are ready to compete from the rest. Rasheed Walker and 2026 first round draft pick Monroe Freeling are maybe the most capable backups the Panthers have ever had at the same time. Both look capable of starting for a lot of teams. Here? They are just holding down the fort. Instead of an injury to a third round pick screwing over all of our hopes and dreams for the wide receivers corps, Brazzell’s injury just clarified the training camp battle for the deepest room we’ve seen in a minute. Instead of wondering who was going to step up as a number two receiver behind DJ Moore or Steve Smith, we spent training camp arguing over who would take the fifth and sixth roster spots. There was a large contingent of people, even after Brazzell went down, that thought the team might legitimately keep seven wide receivers. That kind of depth affords the Panthers the opportunity to be pleasantly surprised, instead of dependent upon, any signs of positive development from Xavier Legette. There are still a thousand questions to answer regarding the 2026 regular season. Not least among them is whether or not the team will get off to their near traditional slow start to September. An extra tally in the win column in the next few weeks could make all the difference for the team’s playoff hopes when their competition is the always fluky NFC South. A thousand more questions will arise when the Panthers actually start playing games on Sunday. The one thing we aren’t questioning is the ability of this team to roll with the first round of punches they received. Depth across the entire roster has improved dramatically since Dan Morgan and Dave Canales started working together. Where they go from here is simply the story of the season. That’s a big step up from the foregone conclusion it would have been even three years ago.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 6 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TN - NOVEMBER 15: Thomas Davis #58 of the Carolina Panthers looks over the offense before the snap during a game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on November 15, 2015 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Wesley Hitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #6. Thomas Davis Sr. Panthers stats: 176 games, 1,098 tackles, 87 tackles for loss, 28 sacks, 13 interceptions Career stats: 199 games, 1,216 tackles, 90 tackles for loss, 29 sacks, 13 interceptions Few players in NFL history, let alone Panthers history, have displayed the combination of excellence and resilience as Thomas Davis Sr. His brilliant 16-year NFL career only came about because of his dogged determination to return from three different ACL tears that would have ended most careers. He’s a living reminder of what it means to overcome the obstacles life throws at you, remain positive and optimistic, then work your rear end off to achieve your goals. Davis joined the Panthers in 2005 as a first round pick (No. 14 overall) after a stellar career at Georgia. The Panthers went 11-5 that year with a roster that featured a plethora of veteran linebackers like Will Witherspoon, Dan Morgan, Brandon Short, and Chris Draft. All four of those guys had at least 50 tackles in Davis’s rookie season, but even then he carved out a rotational role appearing in all 16 games with 40 tackles and 1.5 sacks. In 2006 he locked down a starting gig and in the three seasons between 2006 and 2008 he racked up 291 tackles and eight sacks. His 2009 campaign was off to a great start but then he tore his ACL seven games into the season. Back in 2009 returning from a torn ACL was much more of a dicey proposition than it is today. Davis put in the work to rehab and returned to minicamp in June 2010, just seven months after his initial injury. On the second day of minicamp he re-tore the same ACL in a noncontact drill and ended up missing the entire 2010 season while he rehabbed for a second time. He returned in 2011 and in the second game of the season, he tore the same ACL again. It was the third time that ACL had been torn in 23 months. At the time, no professional athlete had been known to return to their sport after tearing the same ACL three times. But there had also never been an athlete like Thomas Davis. In 2012 Davis managed to return to the Panthers for his age-29 season and miraculously began a streak of five consecutive seasons with at least 100 tackles. He made the Pro Bowl in three consecutive years between 2015 and 2017, and was All-Pro First Team in 2015 when the Panthers went 15-1 and reached the Super Bowl. He remained with the Panthers through 2018, his age-35 season, and was still productive with 79 tackles in 12 games. But by 2019 Carolina was ready for a full-scale rebuild and Davis took his veteran know-how to the Chargers for one season followed by his final campaign with Washington. Thomas Davis’s 1,098 tackles is a Panthers franchise record. The Panthers motto is “Keep Pounding”. That’s exactly what Thomas Davis Sr. did throughout his outstanding 14-year career in Carolina, making him one of the most legendary players in team history.

title: Chicago Bears Rivalries Logo Glow-Up was the Star of the Reveal
summary: Have you seen the Chicago Bears’ new “Rivalries” uniforms put out by Nike? My first reaction was that they finally found a good pairing for that orange helmet they came out with a couple years ago. It’s got some fun wrinkles – the vertical stripes, the orange pants, awesome socks. The patch… yeah, sure, let’s […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES - NOVEMBER 7: Quarterback Sid Luckman #42 of the Chicago Bears runs past end Tom Fears #55 of the Los Angeles Rams during a game played on November 7, 1948 at the Los Angeles Coliseum in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Vic Stein /Getty Images) Have you seen the Chicago Bears’ new “Rivalries” uniforms put out by Nike ? My first reaction was that they finally found a good pairing for that orange helmet they came out with a couple years ago. It’s got some fun wrinkles – the vertical stripes, the orange pants, awesome socks. The patch… yeah, sure, let’s throw a patch on there, I guess. We’ll wait to give an official verdict when they play a game with these new duds, but they pass the initial test. Sure. It's a fun uniform concept with some good history elements. Finally found a better use of the orange helmet. #Bears https://t.co/vXLN0M3YRq — Jeff Berckes (Motivated) (@gridironborn) August 25, 2026 However, the real headliner isn’t even on the jersey – it’s the glow-up Nike gave the best logo in team history from the 1940s and 1950s. The bear on top of a giant orange football… or a tiny bear on a regular-sized football? Open to interpretation. Either way, the Bears started using that logo near the end of their greatest stretch in franchise history, led by Hall of Fame quarterback Sid Luckman paired with Hall of Fame coach George Halas. I say glow up because Nike smartly added “CHICAGO” inside the football, and the result is perfection. The Bears used that old logo as their primary marker for a generation before they adopted a white “C” to put on the side of their helmets in 1962. The white C turned orange in 1974 and is used to this day as the primary logo on helmets. The current bear head arrived in 1999 as the secondary logo, taking over as the primary for merchandise (but not the helmet, unfortunately) starting in 2023. I’ll save my discussion for another day on the need to refresh the brand every generation or two so that you can revisit eras like Nike did with this upcycled logo. It’s a lonely hill I’ll defend some other time. For now, I just want to reflect on this awesome logo and what it could mean to us Bears fans in the future. The “Rivalries Logo” enters the scene on the eve of the most anticipated season in quite some time. Chicago has been chasing the combination of elite coaching and quarterback play since Luckman and Halas left the sidelines. While we’ve only read the first chapter of the Ben Johnson-Caleb Williams book, most Bears fans agree that it is going to be a page turner. If this Johnson-Williams pairing takes the Bears back to the promised land, this logo will be associated with this newfound success. Much of the new gear that people will buy and wear during this stretch will feature this new logo. It will be in pictures and videos of fans cheering big victories. It will become part of the backdrop and good vibes will follow when Bears fans see the logo in the wild. Maybe I’m stretching here. Maybe I’m wish-casting, trying to pull some magic from a bygone era forward to the modern day. Maybe there isn’t any significance to the timing of a fresh logo besides the hit to my bank account over the next few months. But maybe, just maybe, this all adds up to something special on the lakefront. Put the ball on the tee and let’s ****ing go.

full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - AUGUST 29: Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears looks on from the sideline during an NFL preseason game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on August 29, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Some of the Windy City Gridiron staff made their picks for several 2026 individual season awards, and we’ll cap the predictions off by picking Super Bowl LXI. We’ve been running through all our picks the last couple of days, and next up is Coach of the Year. Click the link below for any you may have missed. MVP Offensive Player of the Year Defensive Player of the Year Offensive Rookie of the Year Defensive Rookie of the Year Coach of the Year Protector of the Year Super Bowl LXI Bryan Orenchuk: I’m going with Ben Johnson. He wants records broken on offense – we’ll see records broken on offense and one of the most explosive offenses this century as the Chicago Bears firmly establish themselves as contenders under his leadership. Josh Sunderbruch: I want it to be Johnson, but I think it’s going to be Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers. Donald Gooch: Ben Johnson probably should have won it last year, but this year he leads the Bears to a second-division win in the toughest division in football, and he cements himself as one of, if not the, top offensive minds in football. Sam Householder: DeMeco Ryans – The Houston Texans have a very good team, and I think they could break through for a season that turns a lot of heads. Mongo Peanut: Kyle Shanahan. I think he’s going to go toe-to-toe with McVay and end up winning the division with a more flawed roster. This alone should win him the right. TJ Starman: Jesse Minter is my choice for coach of the year. I don’t think there’s an obvious team that was in the depths last season that will rise up this year, but Minter should be able to revitalize a talented Baltimore Ravens roster and get the most out of them. Erik Duerrwaechter: I’d argue Ben Johnson was snubbed last year in his first-ever season as a head coach. In year two, the league will learn to fear and appreciate him for the greatness he’s capable of achieving. Gary Baugher Jr.: Always the toughest to forecast because usually it goes to a coach who facilitated a turnaround with a bad team. So, of the new hires (or previous coaches who find themselves on new teams), I like the situation John Harbaugh is in. The defense is a top-half unit overall, and if he can unlock Dart more, I can see a 9-10 win season from the Giants with their 4th-place schedule. Lester A. Wiltfong Jr.: Minter will take the Ravens from a sub .500 team back to the playoffs, which is the kind of thing voters look for. Jeff Berckes: Sometimes this goes to the coach of a purely dominant team, but so often it goes to a coach that exceeds expectations. As if the media wasn’t wrong in their preseason forecast, and it was an amazing coaching job that lifted the team up. The NFC South has the following over/under win expectations: Panthers 6.5, Saints 7.5, Falcons 7.5, and Buccaneers 8.5. Someone has to win this division, and I’d be willing to put a dollar on the Saints emerging and Kellen Moore taking it home. full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - AUGUST 29: Skyler Thomas #38 of the Chicago Bears looks on during the second half of the Week 3 preseason game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on August 29, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images On her latest Making Monsters, Taylor Doll interviews Coach Rod Chance, who coached Chicago Bears undrafted free agent safety Skyler Thomas at Oregon State. Thomas had a really solid camp and performed well in the preseason, and he made Chicago’s opening 53-man roster. There were times this offseason when he was running with the ones, so he may be a bigger part of the Bears’ future than a typical UDFA. Coach Chance shares thoughts on Skyler’s versatility, his strengths, and, most importantly, his personality on and off the football field. Chance also coached at Minnesota, Southern Utah, and Oregon, so he shared some thoughts on several other Bears he coached or coached against, like Braxton Jones, Noah Sewell, Rome Odunze, and Dillion Thieneman. But as for Thomas, he was a huge asset for Coach Chance when the Beavers hired him as their secondary coach in 2024. Thomas was hurt in 2023, so he spent that year in the booth charting the defense and helping the coaches, and he shared that knowledge of the D with Chance, who was hired just a couple of days before spring ball started. “He’s got great respect for who he is as a person,” Coach said about Thomas. “He is a person that truly does everything one way, which is the best of his ability. Never was a time where he wasn’t the first person in the building, the first person in the meeting room; if I sent a group text message out he’s the first person to respond to that. The 3.89 GPA as a student-athlete, and as you guys know, he’s married, so he kind of had his game plan of life all together. And that’s a credit to his family. His mom and dad, they both did a great job kind of working together to raise him, and those characteristics kind of showed up in who he was as a person on a day-to-day basis.” He goes on to explain how Thomas was used at Oregon State, his leadership on and off the field, and so much more. title: Bengals Tuesday Trenches: It begins with Pirates
summary: The 2026 NFL season is here. The wait is over. The Cincinnati Bengals will take the field Sunday at Paycor Stadium against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in a game that actually matters. And it does matter. Unlike the MLB or the NBA, which both have absurdly long regular seasons, the NFL (for now) plays only 17 games. That […]
full_text: Dec 18, 2022; Tampa, Florida, USA; Tampa Bay Buccaneers linebacker Lavonte David (54) sacks Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) during the second quarter at Raymond James Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kim Klement-USA TODAY Sports The 2026 NFL season is here. The wait is over. The Cincinnati Bengals will take the field Sunday at Paycor Stadium against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in a game that actually matters. And it does matter. Unlike the MLB or the NBA, which both have absurdly long regular seasons, the NFL (for now) plays only 17 games. That means every game—from the first to the last—is important. The Bengals are contenders, and if they want the road to the AFC Championship to go through Cincinnati, they can’t afford to take games off. Cincy has an easy schedule this year. While I don’t think the Bucs are one of the best teams in the league, I do think they’re a top-five team the Bengals will face. I also think the Bengals are better than the Buccaneers, especially on offense. There aren’t many defenses in the league that can consistently keep up with Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins, and the ridiculous number of weapons at Burrow’s disposal. And I think the Bengals’ much-improved defense will make at least a stop or two. Having said all that, I don’t expect the Bengals’ offense to be in midseason form right out of the gate. Any supercar needs a couple of laps to warm up. I was also wrong about Baker Mayfield. When he was drafted, I thought he was a clown. And, from the outside looking in, pretty much anything happening in Cleveland resembles a burning dumpster. But once Mayfield got out of there, my opinion started to change. He’s since revitalized his career, and he’s become a pretty hard guy not to root for. Except for this week. He’ll be able to move the ball against the Bengals, and Tampa Bay has enough offensive firepower to make Cincinnati pay for mistakes. The unsung hero for the Bengals could be Chase Brown. If I’m a defensive coordinator facing the Burrow-Chase-Higgins trifecta, I’m focusing the vast majority of my attention on them. Chase has to be doubled almost all the time, and Higgins can’t consistently be left one-on-one either. Then there’s a third receiver, Mike Gesicki, Erick All Jr., or somebody else waiting to take advantage. The fact is, if the offensive line gives Burrow time to throw, someone is going to get open. That leaves Tampa Bay with two basic options: put as many defensive backs on the field as possible, or pin their ears back and try to get to Burrow before one of his weapons gets open. That’s where Brown could come in. If the Buccaneers load up on defensive backs, Brown could take advantage of a lighter box. And one of the best ways to slow down an aggressive pass rush is to make it pay with an effective running game. I don’t think the Bengals need to “establish the run” to set up the pass, but it’d certainly be nice to see them punish defenses for selling out to stop Burrow. They’ve spent a lot of time working with Burrow under center and adding more play action into the offense. If they can pull that off effectively, it could buy Burrow the extra second he needs to find one of his many weapons downfield. The guy the Bengals’ offense needs to keep an eye on is Rueben Bain Jr. Had the Bengals not traded the No. 10 overall pick to the Giants for Dexter Lawrence II, Bain is the guy I would have wanted Cincinnati to select. As it turns out, they’ll face him in Week 1. There hasn’t been a Buccaneers defender with double-digit sacks since the 2021 season, and they’re hoping Bain can help snap that streak. The Bengals would probably prefer he starts his push in Week 2. For Cincinnati’s defense, all eyes are on the defensive line. Last year, the starters were B.J. Hill and T.J. Slaton. Now, Hill and Slaton are the backups, while Lawrence and Jonathan Allen are starting. Throw in Kris Jenkins and rookie Landon Robinson, and suddenly the Bengals have a deep and talented defensive interior—something they’ve desperately lacked over the last few seasons. That group could make all the difference Sunday. If the Bengals can get consistent pressure from Boye Mafe and Myles Murphy while Lawrence, Allen and company collapse the pocket from the interior, Mayfield could be forced to get rid of the ball early or throw off-platform. That creates opportunities for Cincinnati’s linebackers and defensive backs to make plays. So, whose defense steps up the most? Vegas lists the Bengals as 3.5-point favorites, which is basically home-field advantage plus another half-point. I’ll take those odds. I see a close game that is somewhat frustrating at times. It’s Week 1. There will probably be some rust, some missed opportunities, and at least one moment that makes Bengals fans collectively wonder why they allow this team to do this to them every year. But I think Cincinnati wins. Bengals 27, Buccaneers 20. It might not be pretty, but being 1-0 is all that matters. Who do you think wins? Sound off! Who Dey, and welcome to what we will hopefully look back on as the first game of the greatest season in Bengals franchise history! title: Al Golden’s confidence in Cashius Howell says a lot about the Bengals’ promising rookie
summary: There is no shortage of excitement surrounding Cincinnati Bengals rookie defensive end Cashius Howell. And if defensive coordinator Al Golden’s assessment of his new pass rusher is any indication, the Bengals may have landed a player who can make an impact much sooner than some might expect. When Cincinnati selected Howell with the 41st overall pick in […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - AUGUST 13: Cincinnati Bengals defensive end Cashius Howell (55) recovers a Lions fumble during the game between the Detroit Lions and the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images There is no shortage of excitement surrounding Cincinnati Bengals rookie defensive end Cashius Howell. And if defensive coordinator Al Golden’s assessment of his new pass rusher is any indication, the Bengals may have landed a player who can make an impact much sooner than some might expect. When Cincinnati selected Howell with the 41st overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, the reaction was largely centered around one obvious trait: production. Howell recorded 11.5 sacks and 14 tackles for loss during his final season at Texas A&M, earning SEC Defensive Player of the Year honors and first-team All-America recognition. He finished his college career with 27 sacks and 35.5 tackles for loss. But Golden sees more than just a player who knows how to get to the quarterback. “Dynamic pass rusher, great production — not average production, great production,” Golden said after the Bengals selected Howell. That distinction is important. The Bengals didn’t simply draft Howell because he put up impressive numbers at Texas A&M. They believe those numbers are the product of a skill set that can translate to Cincinnati’s defense. Golden specifically pointed to Howell’s versatility. He can rush from a traditional edge position. He can line up as an outside linebacker. He can play in different fronts. He has shown that he can drop into coverage. And, perhaps most importantly for a Bengals defense looking to create more pressure, he gives Golden another option when it comes time to attack opposing quarterbacks. “He can play 4-2 edge, can play outside backer if you go to bigger people,” Golden said. “Showed proficiency with the ability to drop. Can help us on special teams. So, this is a multifaceted athlete and a really twitched-up guy.” That’s a strong endorsement. And it helps explain why Cincinnati reportedly viewed Howell so highly on its draft board. The Bengals had to wait until the second round to make their first selection, yet Howell was still sitting there at No. 41. Cincinnati’s decision-makers didn’t appear to view that as a problem. They viewed it as an opportunity. Assistant general manager Mike Potts called Howell’s ability to win quickly as a pass rusher “really dynamic.” At the same time, the Bengals’ draft team reportedly had Howell as the highest player remaining on its board. Following a recent practice, Golden continued to heap praise on Howell, noting that his intelligence has really helped the rookie transition to the pro level. “Hitting on Cashius, I can’t underscore how important that is because he’s come through for us in terms of his intellect, his work ethic, his ability to process, and his learning curve,” Golden told Paul Dehner Jr. of The Athletic . Golden’s comments reinforce the idea that Cincinnati wasn’t simply drafting for depth. The Bengals were adding another weapon. A Different Kind of Edge Rusher One of the more intriguing aspects of Howell’s fit in Cincinnati is his physical profile. At roughly 6-foot-2 and 253 pounds, Howell isn’t the prototypical long, towering defensive end. His arms measured just over 30 inches at the combine, something that became a major talking point during the pre-draft process. But the Bengals clearly weren’t overly concerned. They saw the burst, the bend, and the pass-rush arsenal. And they saw a player who consistently found ways to get home. Howell’s game is built around his ability to get off the ball and attack. That’s precisely the kind of skill set Golden can move around the formation and utilize in different situations. That versatility becomes even more interesting when you consider the rest of Cincinnati’s defensive line. The Bengals now have Howell alongside players such as Shemar Stewart, Myles Murphy, Boye Mafe, and Dexter Lawrence II. That’s a very different-looking group than the one Cincinnati had a year ago. And Howell doesn’t necessarily have to be the centerpiece of it. He can be the chess piece. Golden specifically compared Howell’s body type to Mafe’s and talked about the variety the two can provide on early downs and in obvious passing situations. That could be where Howell becomes particularly dangerous. The Production Is Already There There’s always going to be a learning curve for a rookie defensive lineman entering the NFL. But Howell isn’t coming to Cincinnati as some developmental project with theoretical upside. He already has a production track record. His 11.5 sacks in 2025 weren’t simply the result of playing a few favorable matchups. He became one of the most disruptive defenders in the SEC and earned the conference’s top defensive player award. That matters. The Bengals have spent years looking for ways to generate more consistent pressure without relying exclusively on one player to win his matchup. Howell gives them another legitimate pass-rush threat. And Golden seems to believe he can do considerably more than just rush the passer. That’s what makes the rookie so intriguing. Golden’s Confidence Should Get Bengals Fans Excited There is a difference between a coach saying nice things about a rookie and a coach describing exactly how that rookie can help his defense. Golden’s comments fall into the second category. He’s already talking about Howell’s ability to play different positions, rush from different alignments, drop into coverage, and contribute on special teams. That’s not the description of a player the Bengals intend to keep in a limited package. It’s the description of a player they believe can become part of the defensive identity. Howell himself has described his projected role as a hybrid edge rusher — playing defensive end on base downs, occasionally dropping into coverage, and being used in various blitz packages. That sounds an awful lot like the type of player Golden wants to have at his disposal. And perhaps that’s the biggest reason to pay attention to the growing buzz around Howell in Cincinnati. The hype isn’t simply coming from draft analysts or fans watching his college tape. It’s coming from the guy who designed the Bengals’ defense. Al Golden clearly believes Cashius Howell can be a difference-maker. Now Bengals fans get to find out just how quickly that belief becomes reality.

They are still figuring out a plan, but “very encouraged and excited” about how he looked today. It’s not like a year ago where everything is new, both technique and concept. From that standpoint the journey shouldn’t be as long to try to get him back.” The good thing about Stewart is the Bengals have plenty of capable bodies on the edge, so there’s no need to rush him back if he’s not ready. full_text: There is a lot of uncertainty about what the Cleveland Browns will look like this season, especially in their Week 1 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Deshaun Watson will make his first regular-season start since 2024, giving Todd Monken his first opportunity to showcase what the offense can look like with the team’s new, young talent. It will be particularly interesting to see how the Jaguars secondary fares against the Browns pass catchers, especially KC Concepcion . Concepcion is known for his route running and separation, and this game will be a good opportunity to see if this skill set continues to show up at NFL game speed. Josh Hines-Allen has had a fantastic career thus far and is likely to continue on this route in 2026. With the shakeup on Cleveland’s offensive line and the uncertainty of how Watson will look under center, Hines-Allen has the chance to really leave his mark on this game. This will be a big “Welcome to the NFL” moment for Spencer Fano as he tries to prove he is ready for his role on the offensive line. Mason Graham enters his second season with 17 games of experience under his belt, which should give him greater confidence heading into the new year. This game will be a big test for him as an interior defensive lineman going up against Trevor Lawrence . If the Browns want to have success in this matchup, it will be important to see how much pressure he can generate on Lawrence early in the game. Let me know what you think in the comments – What is the most important matchup in Browns vs. Jaguars?

title: Did Browns HC Todd Monken tip his hand about the QB rotation?
summary: Cleveland Browns head coach Todd Monken walked into a situation no head coach wants to find themselves in.  When training camp opened, Monken looked at the quarterback room, and staring back at him were broken-down veteran Deshaun Watson, rookie Taylen Green, and second-year players Shedeur Sanders and Dillon Gabriel. Monken’s task, which he very much […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 11: Shedeur Sanders #2, Dillon Gabriel #6 and Taylen Green #15 of the Cleveland Browns look on during the Cleveland Browns Mandatory Minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 11, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images Cleveland Browns head coach Todd Monken walked into a situation no head coach wants to find themselves in. When training camp opened, Monken looked at the quarterback room, and staring back at him were broken-down veteran Deshaun Watson, rookie Taylen Green, and second-year players Shedeur Sanders and Dillon Gabriel. Monken’s task, which he very much chose to accept when he took the job, was to somehow figure out how to name a starting quarterback for the upcoming season. That decision was made before the final preseason game when Monken went with the veteran Watson in an attempt to get something out of a quarterback who has not been good since 2020. With that box checked, the next task was to build out the depth chart to determine who would be Watson’s backup and who would be the emergency third quarterback on game days. Gabriel is out, at least for the first four weeks, after coming down with a back injury after a showcase performance against the Chicago Bears in the final preseason game. This left the obvious choice of naming Sanders as the backup and Green as the emergency quarterback. Or did it? Monken has still not officially declared how things are going to play out on Sunday when the Browns face the Jacksonville Jaguars in their Week 1 tilt. Asked about it on Monday before Cleveland’s first practice of the week, Monken remarked that things may not be as they appear : “Could be (Green as the backup). There could be a package where we have him (in the game). It is possible we could use him.” But the Browns could simply roster all three quarterbacks for the game, which would ensure that Green is there if the situation arises, right? Well, not so fast, according to Monken: “I don’t think…well, if we could afford it, it’d be nice to have five or six quarterbacks up, but three is a lot.” Three is a lot. As in, having three quarterbacks on the active game-day roster is a luxury the Browns may not be able to afford. Now this could just all be gamesmanship on Monken’s part to keep the Jaguars guessing about what the Browns have in store for them on Sunday. Of course, it is doubtful that the Jaguars are losing any sleep over the prospect of facing any of Cleveland’s quarterbacks. Or it could be the latest example of the Browns telling everyone how they view Sanders, which is that he is nowhere near being a starting quarterback and still needs considerable work before they even consider him a viable backup option. Unless Monken comes out and clearly states the depth chart this week, late Sunday morning when the inactives are announced for the game, has the potential to be a spicy time in Browns Town.

title: New QB ranking has Browns Shedeur Sanders the lowest, by a lot
summary: Besides the FV Triangle evaluation and young roster hope, rankings related to the Cleveland Browns are mostly negative, with questions surrounding HC Todd Monken and a lot of concern about the quarterback situation. National power rankings and betting lines all see the Browns near the bottom of the list. The QB position continues to be […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OH - DECEMBER 28: Cleveland Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders (12) talks to Cleveland Browns head coach Kevin Stefanski on the sideline during the second quarter of the National Football League game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and Cleveland Browns on December 28, 2025, at Huntington Bank Field in Cleveland, OH. (Photo by Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Besides the FV Triangle evaluation and young roster hope , rankings related to the Cleveland Browns are mostly negative, with questions surrounding HC Todd Monken and a lot of concern about the quarterback situation. National power rankings and betting lines all see the Browns near the bottom of the list. The QB position continues to be the big concern. The Athletic’s Mike Sando put out his annual QB tier ranking , which saw both Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders in the lowest tier, with the latter last overall. SB Nation’s quarterback data also had Sanders’ performance in 2025 at the bottom of the league. Sando’s list had a quote on Sanders that stuck out as perhaps the most negative of any all offseason: “‘I’d sleep like a baby if I got to play him every week” The Athletic’s new Quarterback Index data point adds to the negativity thrown Sanders’ way. Much like ESPN’s QBR, QBI attempts to put quarterback play into the context of what is within his control and weed out the other factors: QBI is a metric we’ve created that strips away the contributions from a quarterback’s 10 offensive teammates and credits only what the quarterback provides on a per-play basis. Again, it’s not perfect; no QB stats are. But the hope is that QBI provides a better picture of quarterback quality than the traditional stats (passing touchdowns, passing yards, completion rate) as well as the more advanced metrics (EPA and success rate). With Joe Burrow (132) scored at the top and Matthew Stafford and Brock Purdy (125) right behind, we scroll down to 37th, again last, to find Sanders (47). Based on the QBI, Sanders’ 2025 season was about 40% worse than the next quarterbacks: JJ McCarthy (76), Tua Tagovailoa (78), and Cam Ward (78). Whether the blame falls on Sanders, former Cleveland HC Kevin Stefanski, the lack of preparation in college, or some kind of bias, QBI attempts to pull away one of the variables that often gets used as a reason for Sanders’ poor rookie season – his supporting cast. With Watson set to start the season, many believe Sanders will get a chance with a different coach, with more NFL experience, and a better supporting cast. If he does, it will be interesting how QBI and the other rankings change for the young quarterback. What do you think of QBI trying to pull Sanders’ performance away from what his supporting cast did and still coming up with a low score/ranking? title: 3 contract extensions Browns should try to get done this week, all defensive starters
summary: This offseason, the Cleveland Browns had two defenders who, somewhat secretly, held out for new contracts. In short order, GM Andrew Berry locked up CB Denzel Ward and S Grant Delpit, keeping them on the Browns roster for the foreseeable future. With Cleveland back on the field for practice on Monday, before starting up their […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 27: Ronnie Hickman #33 of the Cleveland Browns walks off the field prior to a preseason game against the New England Patriots at Huntington Bank Field on August 27, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images This offseason, the Cleveland Browns had two defenders who, somewhat secretly, held out for new contracts. In short order, GM Andrew Berry locked up CB Denzel Ward and S Grant Delpit , keeping them on the Browns roster for the foreseeable future. With Cleveland back on the field for practice on Monday , before starting up their normal regular-season practice schedule on Wednesday, Berry could look to get a few more contracts handled. As of now, the Browns roster has 17 players set to hit unrestricted free agency at the end of the year. The majority are either stopgaps, backups, or Deshaun Watson . There are three starting defenders on that list, however, who might be smart for Cleveland to lock up: DT Maliek Collins – Recovering from an injury, Collins didn’t practice in training camp but is expected to be ready to go in the early part of the season. One of the oldest players on the Browns roster at 32, Collins was highly impactful in his first season in the orange and brown. A reasonable contract extension for a year or two, especially with Cleveland’s salary cap space , could help create some consistency on the defensive line. S Ronnie Hickman – The former undrafted free agent couldn’t come to an agreement on a long-term deal earlier this offseason, instead signing for just this season before hitting unrestricted free agency. With Emmanuel McNeil-Warren drafted in the second round, the Browns may not want to overpay the Ohio State Buckeyes’ product, but having all three safeties for a few years would really help DC Mike Rutenberg’s system. Again, with a big chunk of cap space available, a Top 20 safety contract would be doable for both sides. DE Isaiah McGuire – The departure of Myles Garrett was softened by the arrival of Jared Verse in the same trade. There is a drop-off between the two, but Verse is a young, proven player. The season-ending injury to Alex Wright created a ripple effect that moved McGuire into the starting lineup and led to the signing of Derek Barnett . If Berry and Rutenberg see a big season coming for McGuire, who has never played in more than 44% of the defense’s snaps, getting a two- to three-year extension done might be in everyone’s best interest. The good news for the Browns is that none of the above extensions are required moves. Cleveland has some depth at defensive tackle, added McNeil-Warren in this year’s draft, and McGuire has been a mostly replacement-level player so far in his career. On the other hand, the Browns have the salary cap space to create some continuity on the defense and make sure Rutenberg and company have depth to work with over the next couple of seasons. full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - NOVEMBER 16: (L-R) Joel Bitonio #75 and Shedeur Sanders #12 of the Cleveland Browns look on during the second half against the Baltimore Ravens at Huntington Bank Field on November 16, 2025 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns are on the cusp of playing their first regular-season game against the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 1. There have been plenty of changes from the coaching staff as well as the roster from last season. New head coach Todd Monken held an open quarterback competition this training camp, which included all four of his signal-callers, but essentially was between veteran Deshaun Watson and the youngster Shedeur Sanders. Eventually, Monken chose Watson as his starter going forward. RELATED: BITONIO POST-RETIREMENT INTERVIEW Was it close? What was Monken’s decision based on? Did the preseason games come into play in that decision? Most likely, Monken’s decision was based on what occurred in practice sessions. The reason behind this assumption is that in each exhibition game, every player on the Browns faced either the opponent’s second-or third-string athletes. Few starters on both sides of the ball even played, so how can an honest eval be conducted against second-teamers? Yet, Cleveland’s offense in practices went up against last year’s #4 defensive unit. That will tell quite a bit. Recently, retired offensive guard Joel Bitonio was a guest on The Bearded Browns Podcast to discuss everything Cleveland Browns. He was asked why he thought Sanders was not named the starting quarterback. Bitonio stated: “ I thought we saw in the preseason his development from last year. But if you look at the little things, like time to throw and pocket awareness, and just — the guys get open and he makes a big play when they’re open. But there’s a little bit of just anticipation and time to throw. ” Here at DBN , we have published several interviews with Bitonio . He played 13 seasons and garnered seven Pro Bowls. He knows his stuff. Last year, he was the only offensive lineman still standing in the final game who started in Week 1. Last season, Sanders played in eight games and started seven. So Bitonio has seen his play up close and personal in live games, as well as getting first-team reps in practices. Sanders has a huge fanbase that transcends the Browns. Go to Facebook and type in “Shedeur Sanders” and see how many pages have been dedicated to his NFL career. He is like Peyton Manning when he graduated from the University of Tennessee and was then drafted by the Indianapolis Colts. Tennessee fans instantly became Colts’ followers. Once Manning left and became the starter with the Denver Broncos, those same fans switched their allegiance to the Broncos. The fanbase of Sanders right now is with Cleveland. His fans state that he is a superstar in waiting and a combination of Tom Brady, Michael Vick, and Johnny Unitas, all rolled into one quarterback. Basically, beyond “generational talent.” They are extremely vocal and cannot understand why the coaching staff doesn’t see this. Of course, for many, their sampling in this year’s training camp was on their TV set, phone, or computer screen, and not in person in practice sessions. On the telecast, the Browns’ second-team offensive line played really well and gave each quarterback a clean pocket with ample time to survey the field. Keep in mind, this was against the other team’s second-team defense. On the above play, Sanders had 6.2 seconds to throw. Four seconds on any passing play is considered an eternity, much less six. The pocket remained clean, and at no time did the walls begin to collapse. That is every NFL quarterback’s dream. Bitonio noticed that Sanders is looking downfield more. But he has a flaw: He isn’t ready and needs more time to develop. Bitonio explained: “ As a lineman, it sucks, but if you’re taking over three seconds to throw in the league, like, I don’t care if you have five Joe Thomases in front of you. It is tough to handle.” The knock-on Sanders is that as long as he has a good pocket, he is a productive quarterback. “I think that anytime Shedeur can take a step back and continue to learn and continue to process, I thought we saw in the preseason his development from last year. It looked significantly better. Continue to learn, continue to process as a young quarterback. It’s great for him.” To hear this information from a guy who actually was in the huddle with Sanders speaks volumes. Bitonio knows. He saw the rookie Sanders and now has watched the sophomore Sanders from afar. What Sanders has had to come to grips with is that he is expected to make a play every time he drops back to pass. This means he isn’t throwing the ball quickly enough, or getting rid of it and living to play another down. This isn’t college. This isn’t the Pac-12 where only three teams you play on the schedule all year have a good pass rush, or the defensive backs are on an elite level. In the NFL, everybody is incredible. The backups are very good. Last year was an awakening period. Sanders, like most or all rookies, came into the NFL not ready for the speed of defenders along the defensive front, as well as in the defensive backfield. But in practices, he gets a dose of Denzel Ward and Tyson Campbell each day. It is like back in the day when the Browns’ receivers had to test Frank Minnifield and Hanford Dixon. INTERVIEW: BROWNS WR BRIAN BRENNAN That alone made guys like Brian Brennan, Webster Slaughter, and Reggie Langhorne have to reach down deep and produce. What about the fact that Sanders is just in his second season, along with Dillon Gabriel, while Watson has been in the league since 2017? Could this have come into play with Monken’s decision to go with Watson over either Sanders or Gabriel? Bitonio said: “The quarterback room overall, the personalities of the young guys, Shedeur and Dillon, are both great guys. Both want to put in the work. Both work hard. Obviously, they found a way to get Dillon on IR for a few weeks. (Shedeur) was a developmental player when they drafted him, and he’s continued to develop. I think they’ve shown good signs. And then Deshaun, that 2023 Ravens game in the second half, that showed fans what the team had hoped he would be. He was a perfect passer. He was scrambling. He was making plays. He helped lead us to a victory. Everybody thought this was the moment when he got his confidence back.” And what about the Browns’ decision to start Watson? Before the franchise mortgaged the farm to trade for him, he was a Top-5 quarterback in the league with three Pro Bowls in his first four seasons. Could his experience be one of the reasons Coach Monken chose Watson over Sanders? Bitonio gave his take on Watson on the Bearded Browns Podcast : “I think he’s shown enough promise with the offense. Coach Monken obviously trusts him the most to go and win games. That’s really the bottom line. Coach Todd Monken is trying to win as many games as possible. And at this current position, he thinks Deshaun Watson is going to get as many wins as possible for him. This might be his only chance to be a head coach in the NFL. He is going to put the guy he thinks is going to win him the most games, and if the time comes, Shedeur will be ready to step in.” Cleveland begins the 2026 season on September 13th on the road against the Jacksonville Jaguars. How are you feeling about Shedeur Sanders’ development so far? What do you think about Joel Bitonio’s thoughts on the 2nd-year QB? Join the conversation! title: The quiet shift reshaping the Cowboys
summary: The Cowboys may have quietly changed what they’re looking for in a football player. Not necessarily bigger. Not necessarily faster. Not necessarily more talented. Just more serious. Call them “Serious Dudes“, with a hat tip to Voch Lombardi for the moniker. It’s not a scientific category, and it’s certainly not a requirement that every player […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - DECEMBER 14: The Dallas Cowboys huddle during the game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Minnesota Vikings on December 14, 2025 at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Matthew Pearce/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cowboys may have quietly changed what they’re looking for in a football player. Not necessarily bigger. Not necessarily faster. Not necessarily more talented. Just more serious. Call them “ Serious Dudes “, with a hat tip to Voch Lombardi for the moniker . It’s not a scientific category, and it’s certainly not a requirement that every player walk around the facility looking like he’s preparing for a tax audit. It’s more about how a player approaches the job: preparation, accountability, doing his assignment, competing through the whistle, and not needing every moment to become a personal statement. The Cowboys have always had players like that. Every successful team does. What’s interesting is how many of them now seem to be showing up on this roster. And that makes me wonder whether Brian Schottenheimer has quietly started putting more emphasis on a quality that doesn’t show up particularly well on a draft board or salary-cap spreadsheet: professionalism. The new generation of Cowboys Start with Tyler Booker: The second-year guard was identified as a natural leader before he had even played his first NFL season, then followed that up with more than 1,000 snaps and 14 starts as a rookie. Now, just one year into his career, Booker is already part of the Cowboys’ 11-man Leadership Council . That’s not necessarily because he’s the loudest player in the room. It’s because the organization appears to trust him to help set the standard. Then there’s Caleb Downs. Downs is an even more interesting case because the expectations attached to him go well beyond simply playing good football. Dallas traded up to select Downs 11th overall, and the conversation around him quickly became about influence as much as ability. Mel Kiper called him a “ culture changer ,” while NFL.com’s Lance Zierlein described him as a “ culture piece ” for a Dallas defense that badly needed one. But perhaps the most telling assessment came from inside the Cowboys’ locker room. When DeMarvion Overshown was asked about Downs, he didn’t talk about giving a rookie time to adjust to the NFL. He said the Cowboys weren’t even looking at Downs as a rookie. They were looking at him as someone who could “change this defense around” and “change the culture.” That’s a remarkable expectation to place on a player who hasn’t yet played an NFL snap. And it tells us something about what the Cowboys think they drafted. Downs isn’t simply expected to be a good safety. He’s expected to be an influence. Of course, Downs hasn’t yet established himself as a locker-room leader. But the Cowboys expected that potential to be part of his value when they traded up to get him. And then there is the rest of the next generation. Jaishawn Barham might be the clearest example of the type. The rookie linebacker was one of the more talked-about players in training camp, and the description coming from the Cowboys themselves was almost tailor-made for this post: “ all business. ” Schottenheimer also highlighted Barham’s physicality, his ability to get off blocks, and his versatility. Malachi Lawrence is a quieter example. The first-round pick hasn’t attracted anything like the attention surrounding Downs, but his early approach has been refreshingly straightforward: learn from the veterans, understand what it means to be a professional, and work on the technical details of his game. That doesn’t prove Lawrence will become a leader in Dallas. It doesn’t even tell us what kind of personality he’ll have five years from now. But it is another example of the type of player the Cowboys appear to be bringing into the building. Donovan Ezeiruaku is a slightly different case. There is plenty of evidence of the work ethic and football intelligence Dallas likes, and the second-year edge rusher has talked about the importance of standards and learning from veterans . The Cowboys’ training-camp coverage has also highlighted his knowledge and experience. But Ezeiruaku also plays with an edge. His involvement in several training-camp fights was a reminder that taking football seriously doesn’t necessarily mean being emotionless. A Serious Dude doesn’t have to be boring. He can be intense. He can be emotional. He can be loud. The distinction is what happens when the helmet comes off. The veterans who changed the locker room The pattern becomes more visible when you look at the veterans Dallas added. Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark are probably the two strongest examples. Neither needed the Cowboys to teach them how to be professionals. They came with established reputations, extensive NFL experience, and Pro Bowl credentials. Yet both quickly became central figures in the locker room. Williams arrived in the middle of last season, when the Cowboys’ defense was already in trouble. Nine months later, he has been elected one of only four team captains by his teammates . Clark was also voted a captain. The other two are Dak Prescott and Brandon Aubrey. That’s worth noting because the Cowboys have made a distinction this year between their Leadership Council and their team captains. The four captains were chosen entirely by player vote, with Prescott, Williams, Clark, and Aubrey receiving the most votes. Williams has also been unusually open about what he sees changing. After spending the final seven games of 2025 in a defense that was struggling badly, Williams recently described the defense’s progress as “ night and day. ” He credited the coaching, the talent, the daily competition, and the overall change in the way the unit approaches its work. That’s exactly the sort of thing that makes the Serious Dude theory interesting. It’s not just about individual personalities. It’s about what happens when you put enough of the right people together. Kenny Clark fits the same mold. Williams has talked about Clark as someone who holds people accountable and does things the right way, both on and off the field. Jalen Thompson provides another piece of the puzzle. The veteran safety was brought in to stabilize a secondary that badly needed it and was subsequently included in the Leadership Council. Rashan Gary adds another veteran presence to the defensive front, while Cobie Durant brings experience, versatility, and toughness to the secondary. Jonathan Bullard and Otito Ogbonnia are less obvious examples of the personality argument, but they matter in another way: they are experienced defensive linemen who add depth around Williams and Clark. And that’s an important distinction. Not every new player has to be a Serious Dude in the same sense. Some are simply evidence of a roster being built around more experience, physicality, versatility, and professionalism. The pattern emerges from the combination. Meet the Leadership Council Perhaps the most tangible evidence that this is about more than individual impressions is the Cowboys’ Leadership Council. The 11-player group consists of: Dak Prescott CeeDee Lamb Tyler Smith Tyler Booker Jake Ferguson Javonte Williams Quinnen Williams Kenny Clark Rashan Gary Jalen Thompson Bryan Anger That’s an interesting collection of players. It’s also interesting because Schottenheimer has made clear that this isn’t just a ceremonial group. He has said that the council could have included as many as 15 players, but he deliberately kept it smaller. More importantly, he described it as “ their council, it’s not mine. ” The players are expected to bring issues from the locker room to the coaching staff and help solve problems before they become bigger problems. That’s a very different concept from simply naming a few captains for the coin toss. And it tells us something about what the Cowboys value in their leaders. You don’t need to be the…

title: Cowboys news: All eyes on T.J. Bass stepping in for Tyler Smith at LG
summary: The Dallas Cowboys are going to be without all-world left guard Tyler Smith for at least the first four weeks of the season, something head coach Brian Schottenheimer announced on Monday. Coach Schotty also confirmed it will be T.J. Bass starting in Smith’s spot. The biggest phase of the game the Cowboys will miss Smith […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - DECEMBER 21: T.J. Bass #66 of the Dallas Cowboys lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Chargers at AT&T Stadium on December 21, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys are going to be without all-world left guard Tyler Smith for at least the first four weeks of the season, something head coach Brian Schottenheimer announced on Monday. Coach Schotty also confirmed it will be T.J. Bass starting in Smith’s spot. The biggest phase of the game the Cowboys will miss Smith in is his run blocking, with the Cowboys also counting on a repeat performance by Javonte Williams at running back, and sorting out the pecking order behind with Malik Davis and Emari Demercado. Cowboys LG Tyler Smith to undergo thumb surgery, miss 4-6 weeks – Nick Shook, NFL.com A huge blow to the Cowboys offensive line just ahead of two divisional games to start the season. The three-time Pro Bowl guard and cornerstone of Dallas’ interior offensive line was not seen at Monday’s practice, leading to questions regarding his status. With the entire regular season ahead and the thumb injury limiting Smith, the guard felt now was the best time to have the issue fixed, per Schottenheimer. “Just at the end of the day, he felt like he couldn’t do the things he had to do at a high level,” the coach said Monday. “We know this is a long season. It’s unfortunate but that’s why we coveted T.J. Bass and having T.J. Bass back. I think he’s played a lot of really good football for us, and we expect that he’ll continue to do so.” Cowboys have a ‘ton of confidence’ in T.J. Bass filling in for Tyler Smith – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com T.J. Bass has been called on and played well before, and the Cowboys will need more of it as he starts the season at left guard. During training camp, Bass would often times get work with the first-team offensive line in team drills when Schottenheimer and the Cowboys staff would give Smith less snaps in order to manage his workload as a veteran. Schottenheimer hopes those reps will pay off in a game setting. “Offensive line play is tied together,” Schottenheimer said. “We’ve gone into games with four new starters on the offensive line. I’m very, very confident that this group will play well against a really good front. I have great confidence in T.J. Bass. He’s extremely bright, very physical, great athlete. He’ll do a marvelous job for us, I’m sure, stepping in.” What T.J. Bass’ stats tell us about replacing Tyler Smith – Brandon Loree, Blogging The Boys Bass is a player the team can trust to not allow quarterback Dak Prescott to take unnecessary hits. Despite average overall stats for his position, the Cowboys could hang their hat on how efficient Bass was in limited reps. He started in games against the Green Bay Packers, New York Jets, Carolina Panthers, Los Angeles Chargers, and Washington Commanders. He allowed zero sacks last year (T-1st among all 82 guards), had four pressures allowed (second best), and a 99.0 pass-blocking efficiency grade (first). A small sample size to be sure, but he acquitted himself very well. Brian Schottenheimer raises important question about Cowboys offense by answering another – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z Sports Not having Tyler Smith at left guard will put a bigger magnifying glass on Tyler Guyton at left tackle, who the Cowboys will need to stay healthy to avoid going into the further depths of their OL backups. This is a big mystery for a Cowboys offense preparing to start a left tackle who has dealt with injuries in his first couple of NFL seasons. It’s a significant question, and Dallas does not have a firm answer right now. When push comes to shove, I think the Cowboys would end up giving Jones a shot at left tackle. But right now it doesn’t sound like they’re giving him swing tackle treatment. Emari Demercado may be more than just the Cowboys’ third RB – Jess Haynie, The Landry Hat It will be fun to see how RB Emari Demercado’s role develops as the season goes on. When Dallas added Demercado, his profile immediately sounds like a prototypical backup for Javonte Williams . He’s a patient runner with good vision, not adverse to contact while also having breakaway speed . He’s also a proficient receiver and pass blocker, both especially valuable for whoever spells Williams on third-down plays. Demercado is also noted as a “four-core” special teams player, meaning he can play on every unit. This is also a positive point on Davis’ resume, further showing their similarity. Giants cut Darius Slayton – Michael David Smith, Pro Football Talk A roster move for Dallas’ week one opponent ahead of Sunday night. The move comes as a surprise if only because of Slayton’s contract: Just last year, he signed a three-year, $36 million contract, and he is guaranteed $9.75 million this year. Cutting him only saves the Giants $2.5 million, but apparently they’re down enough on him that they thought that savings was worth sending him packing. The Giants presumably tried to trade Slayton before cutting him and found that no one wanted to trade for that contract. Daily discussion question: Which player on the Giants concerns you the most?

title: What T.J. Bass’ stats tell us about replacing Tyler Smith
summary: Before the 2026 season even starts, the Dallas Cowboys are facing their first challenge. Head coach Brian Schottenheimer announced on Monday that All-Pro left guard Tyler Smith is set to undergo surgery on his thumb and will be out for 4-6 weeks. In his place, the Cowboys will go with veteran backup T.J. Bass, who […]
full_text: Before the 2026 season even starts, the Dallas Cowboys are facing their first challenge. Head coach Brian Schottenheimer announced on Monday that All-Pro left guard Tyler Smith is set to undergo surgery on his thumb and will be out for 4-6 weeks. In his place, the Cowboys will go with veteran backup T.J. Bass, who has started in ten games over his career and played the most in a season last year, starting in five games. Cowboys head coach Brain Schottenheimer says Pro Bowl guard Tyler Smith will have surgery on his thumb tomorrow morning. He'll be placed on IR/designated to return and miss 4-6 weeks. pic.twitter.com/yrZnX4zSwL — Tommy Yarrish (@tommy_yarrish) September 7, 2026 Bass is not on the level of Smith, just facts. Very few in the NFL are close to Smith’s level of dominance. However, Bass is the perfect type of player for a situation like this based on his experience in live game situations, and with his knowledge of the offense, having been with Dallas since 2023. Among all NFL guards last season to play at least 20 percent of the snaps, Bass had a 67.6 grade from Pro Football Focus. That ranked 31st out of 82 guards. His pass blocking and run blocking grades were also middle of the pack. “I think he’s [Bass] played a lot of really good football for us, and we expect he’ll continue to do so.” Schottenheimer said during his press conference. Despite average overall stats for his position, the Cowboys could hang their hat on how efficient Bass was in limited reps. He started in games against the Green Bay Packers, New York Jets, Carolina Panthers, Los Angeles Chargers, and Washington Commanders. He allowed zero sacks last year (T-1st among all 82 guards), had four pressures allowed (second best), and a 99.0 pass-blocking efficiency grade (first). A small sample size to be sure, but he acquitted himself very well. It is an unfortunate scenario to start the season, but among the various different spots on the team an injury like this could occur, having it be one where the Cowboys actually have a quality depth player is the silver lining. Bass allows the Cowboys to continue having full confidence in their offense.
