title: What the Christian Gonzalez extension means for the Patriots
summary: Christian Gonzalez finally is the highest-paid cornerback in the NFL. On Monday night, the star defender and the New England Patriots reached an agreement on a four-year extension with a total value of $135 million, a deal that bests Seahawks CB Devon Witherspoon’s deal from earlier this offseason. Besides putting Gonzalez on top of the […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JANUARY 18: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots lines up during an NFC Divisional Playoff game against the Houston Texans at Gillette Stadium on January 18, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Christian Gonzalez finally is the highest-paid cornerback in the NFL. On Monday night, the star defender and the New England Patriots reached an agreement on a four-year extension with a total value of $135 million , a deal that bests Seahawks CB Devon Witherspoon’s deal from earlier this offseason. Besides putting Gonzalez on top of the highest-paid players list at his position, what else does the pact mean? Let’s find out. Elite player locked up Gonzalez is one of the top three cornerbacks in football, a player capable of locking own an opponents’ top wide receiver for four quarters. Having a player of this quality in the fold makes every defense better, and the Patriots’ is obviously no exception. His presence in the team’s backfield cannot be understated. Gonzalez is a true blue-chip defender due to his man-to-man skills and ability to successfully operate in zone as well. Among qualifying CBs, he led the NFL in fewest yards allowed per target in 2025 (5.2) and was voted to his first Pro Bowl. Gonzalez’s abilities allow New England to be aggressive with their coverage calls, which in turn has a trickle-down effect on all other areas as well and effectively allows one player to be removed from the offensive equation. Now, he is being compensated accordingly. Cornerback future secured A true No. 1 cornerback, Gonzalez is the key to the position for the Patriots. As long as he is around, the group has a baseline of quality that instantly puts it high up in any league-wide comparison. And with the 24-year-old now supposedly under contract through 2031 — if the team used a similar structure as the aforementioned Devon Witherspoon deal — New England is in good shape from a long-term perspective. Overall, the current position group and its contract statuses now look as follows: Christian Christian: Signed through 2031 (2032 UFA) Carlton Davis III: Signed through 2027 (2028 UFA) Marcus Jones: Signed through 2028 (2029 UFA) Charles Woods: Signed through 2026 (2027 RFA) Karon Prunty: Signed through 2029 (2030 UFA) Channing Canada: Signed through 2028 (2029 RFA) Kindle Vildor (PS): Signed through 2026 (2027 UFA) Even before the Gonzalez deal, the Patriots’ starting trio of him, Carlton Davis and Marcus Jones was under contract for two more seasons. However, the new pact now creates more stability at the top with top outside option Gonzalez and top slot Jones under team control through 2028 now. Positive signal Robert Kraft’s statements at the start of training camp about the Gonzalez negotiations raised quite a few eyebrows. The Patriots owner publicly said that his team had a deal on the table that would make the fourth-year cornerback the highest-paid player at his position — seemingly trying to shape the narrative surrounding the talks in his organization’s favor. However, multiple subsequent reports as recent as Monday cast doubt over the Patriots’ true intentions. It remains to be seen what the structure of the Gonzalez deal actually looks like, but the fact that he did sign is in itself a positive for a multitude of reasons. Among them is the Patriots staying true to their word; Gonzalez is indeed the highest-compensated cornerback in football now. With the team about to enter even more consequential negotiations soon — quarterback Drake Maye is eligible for an extension starting in January 2027 — the franchise has sent an encouraging signal: the oft-mentioned draft-and-develop approach is not just lip service. Nine-year streak over Do you remember the last time the Patriots signed one of their first-round draft picks to an extension? It happened in 2017, when linebacker Dont’a Hightower — the 25th overall choice in 2012 — put his signature under a four-year, $35.5 million pact. Since then, every one of New England’s first-round selections has left before getting a second contract. The list is bleak, and one of the reasons why the organization dropped off in the early 2020s before hitting rock bottom with back-to-back 4-13 seasons in 2023 and 2024. Before Gonzalez, it included the likes of Dominique Easley (2014), Malcom Brown (2015), Isaiah Wynn (2018), Sony Michel (2018), N’Keal Harry (2019), Mac Jones (2021) and Cole Strange (2022). Out of those seven first-rounders, only two — Brown and Wynn — even made it to the end of their rookie deals. Now, nine years after the Hightower deal, the Patriots have finally signed another of their former Day 1 selections to a new contract. Contract structure TBD As of Tuesday morning, we only know three things about the Gonzalez deal: it’s length, base value, and total guarantees. Everything else has yet to become public knowledge, meaning that some key parameters are missing. We don’t know the cap numbers yet, for example, and also how much of the pact is fully-guaranteed at signing. How will his current pact through 2027 be impacted by the change? Are there void years as with Seahawks’ deal with Witherspoon? What is the incentive structure? Until all of those uncertainties get addressed, we cannot fully assess what the deal means for New England. That being said, the most important facts we know: the two sides reached an agreement to keep working together for multiple years.

title: Christian Gonzalez signs record-breaking contract extension with Patriots
summary: The New England Patriots and Christian Gonzalez have finally reached agreement on a contract extension. After months of negotiations, the two sides found common ground on a record-breaking four-year, $135 million deal. Gonzalez’s contract also includes $102 million in guarantees, another new high for a cornerback. NFL insider Jordan Schultz was first to report the […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 08: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots runs on the field prior to Super Bowl LX against the Seattle Seahawks at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots and Christian Gonzalez have finally reached agreement on a contract extension. After months of negotiations, the two sides found common ground on a record-breaking four-year, $135 million deal. Gonzalez’s contract also includes $102 million in guarantees, another new high for a cornerback. NFL insider Jordan Schultz was first to report the deal. Gonzalez, 24, originally entered the league as the 17th overall selection in the first round of the 2023 NFL Draft. The Oregon product immediately earned a starting role in New England’s secondary, but a season-ending shoulder injury limited his rookie campaign to only four games. Nonetheless, he was able to show considerable promise along the way. Returning without limitations in 2024, the young cornerback took his game to a new level and proved himself as one of the NFL’s best players at his position — a status that was only solidified in his third season in 2025: Gonzalez played a key role in the Patriots returning to the playoffs and advancing to the Super Bowl. In total, he has started all 38 of his combined regular season and playoff games in the NFL so far. Gonzalez has given up only three touchdowns while registering four interceptions and a fumble return for his first career score. He was also named second-team All-Pro in 2024 and voted to the Pro Bowl in 2025.

title: Patriots-Christian Gonzalez contract negotiations reportedly ‘nowhere’
summary: With the NFL season opener approaching fast, the New England Patriots and their best defender, cornerback Christian Gonzalez, have yet to reach common ground in their contract negotiations. In fact, it seems that the two sides remain significantly apart. Appearing on ESPN’s Pat McAfee Show on Monday, NFL insider Adam Schefter painted a bleak picture. […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - JUNE 09: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots speaks to the media after New England Patriots Minicamp on June 9, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images With the NFL season opener approaching fast, the New England Patriots and their best defender, cornerback Christian Gonzalez, have yet to reach common ground in their contract negotiations. In fact, it seems that the two sides remain significantly apart. Appearing on ESPN’s Pat McAfee Show on Monday, NFL insider Adam Schefter painted a bleak picture. “These things always can change. But as of right now, talks are nowhere,” he said. "As of right now the talks are nowhere.. I was told yesterday that a Christian Gonzalez deal wasn't close.. If you can't agree on the money the years become secondary" ~ @AdamSchefter #PMSLive pic.twitter.com/oCzikDh7Kx — Pat McAfee (@PatMcAfeeShow) September 7, 2026 “There always can be a last-second push and there always can be something that changes,” Schefter continued. “We’ll see how the two sides address it once the season’s underway. But I think, as of right now, it’s hard to imagine that the two sides would be able to make up the difference to get a deal done by opening night. We’ve seen crazy things happen, and I’m sure there could be another push to try to see if they could salvage it and get it done. But right now, as of yesterday, I was told it was not close. We’ll see if they can figure out anything by the start of the game. It didn’t sound like that was going to be the case.” The Patriots’ first-round draft pick in 2023, Gonzalez has been one of the NFL’s top cornerbacks since entering the league. As a result, the 24-year-old is looking to become the league’s highest-paid player in the league at his position — something the organization, by its own admission, is willing to support. At the moment, that title belongs to Devon Witherspoon. A fellow 2023 draft pick, Witherspoon signed a four-year, $132 million extension with the Seattle Seahawks earlier this offseason. In terms of average annual value ($33M) and total guarantees ($101M), no cornerback has ever been above the three-time Pro Bowler. Gonzalez, according to Schefter, is looking to at least match Witherspoon. However, the Patriots — despite statements to the contrary by both team owner Robert Kraft and de facto general manager Eliot Wolf — apparently “have never been there” and “have not gotten close to there.” Time will tell how accurate that information is, and whether or not the Patriots will reach a common ground after all. There is at least one NFL insider, though, who thinks so: Benjamin Allbright of KOA Colorado posted on Sunday that a “deal eventually will get done.”

title: Patriots preparing to go soundless in Seattle to start the new season
summary: Seattle’s Lumen Field is one of the loudest stadiums in pro football already, but the 12s might take it up a notch come Wednesday night. Not only will their team open the 2026 NFL season at home, it also will unveil its Super Bowl banner earned in February. That banner, of course, was earned at […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - DECEMBER 28: Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots under center during the game against the New York Jets on December 28, 2025 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Seattle’s Lumen Field is one of the loudest stadiums in pro football already, but the 12s might take it up a notch come Wednesday night. Not only will their team open the 2026 NFL season at home, it also will unveil its Super Bowl banner earned in February. That banner, of course, was earned at the detriment of the New England Patriots. And those very same Patriots will have a front-row seat to the Seahawks’ celebration, which also means they get an opportunity to play spoilers. In order to do so, however, overcoming a tough environment will be crucial. And in order to do so and get a more satisfying result especially on the offensive side of the ball, New England will be relying on a silent snap count extensively. For Drake Maye and company, one of the secrets to success is being soundless in Seattle. “There’s advantages and disadvantages to working in the silent, and I think it’s mostly just us repping it,” said Maye. “Coach [Mike] Vrabel and the offensive staff do a great job of preparing us, and I think we got a lot of work at it, and those guys got a good grip on it. So, we got to stay out of penalties, avoid penalties and keep the positive plays going, and I think when we are ahead of the chains, we tend to do better for ourselves.” “I just think it’s the communication and getting guys on the same page,” said Maye’s position coach, Patriots QB coach Ashton Grant. “A lot of what we do is verbal communicating, so when you go into a loud environment where you can’t use your voices, I think just trying to get everyone on the same page when we’re trying to snap the ball and what other communication we’re trying to get done, I think it becomes important.” Now in his third year, Maye is no stranger to using a silent count in a game. The same is true for the experienced offensive line and skill group surrounding him. And yet, at first glance there appears to be an element of uncertainty. With verbal communication not an option, the operation suddenly relies on every player being on the same page timing-wise. As offensive line coach Doug Marrone explained, however, the core elements at play still remain the same. It’s all about focus and responsibility, as would be the case using a normal pre-snap cadence. “I’ve always tried to train myself when I was a player to just be like, ‘Okay, here’s my job. Here’s my responsibility. Okay, here we go. The number one thing I have to do right now is just focus on this on this snap count,’” Marrone explained. “And it doesn’t change really. This is where people may really understand: it’s the same way when we’re doing it with the cadence. It’s that same type of focus that you need. … “For me as a player when I did it, it was a matter of just managing that you know, ‘Here it comes.’ It’s different in college because the best player you played in college, you’re playing every week, and it’s at every position. So, you’re kind of just making sure, like, ‘Look, I’m not going to try to cheat this thing. I’m not going to get it. We’re going to get off at the same time and we’re going to be okay.’” At the end of the day, much of the responsibility for the timing being correct falls on the quarterback and center. In New England’s case, that means relying on a new pairing: while Maye is still calling the shots from the QB position, Jared Wilson is now handling the snaps in place of veteran Garrett Bradbury. While Wednesday’s game will be Wilson’s first as the Patriots’ starting center, offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels is not worried about the offensive operation not being on point. “The quarterback and the center, if they’re not on the same page, [the rest of the offense] doesn’t really matter,” McDaniels said. “So, whatever we talk about with Drake, you kind of also are talking about Jared. They distribute a lot of information to their teammates and they do a really good job of it.”

title: Patriots vs. Seahawks preview for NFL Week 1
summary: The New England Patriots’ 2025 season as a whole was a success, but it ultimately ended in a disappointing loss to the Seattle Seahawks in the Super Bowl. Seven months removed from its 29-13 defeat, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel will get another crack at the newly-crowned world champions: it’s Patriots at Seahawks […]
full_text: SAN JOSE, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 04: A Seattle Seahawks helmet is seen during a practice ahead of Super Bowl LX at San Jose State University on February 04, 2026 in San Jose, California. (Photo by Eakin Howard/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots’ 2025 season as a whole was a success, but it ultimately ended in a disappointing loss to the Seattle Seahawks in the Super Bowl. Seven months removed from its 29-13 defeat, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel will get another crack at the newly-crowned world champions: it’s Patriots at Seahawks to kick off the NFL’s 2026 season. The two teams will face off at Seattle’s Lumen Field on Wednesday night, a highly-anticipated rematch that will feature a new-look Patriots team going up against a steady Seahawks squad that saw only marginal changes during the offseason. The question is whether or not New England managed to close what was a 16-point gap on Super Bowl Sunday. We will find out on Wednesday. For now, let’s get to know the Seahawks in our first opponent preview of the season. Seahawks key stats The Seahawks were the best team in the NFL last season, and their stats reflected this. And given that the personnel turnover has been minimal — more on it in a second — it would not be a surprise to see them post similar numbers in 2026 as well. Given that those numbers are the only serious statistical information we have about the team, if we disregard its 0-2-1 preseason slate, let’s take a look at them. Record: 14-3 (1st NFC West/1st NFC) Scoring differential: +191 (1st) Turnover differential: -3 (t-19th) Offense: 28.4 points/game (3rd), 351.4 yards/game (8th), 28 giveaways (31st), 0.036 EPA/play (14th), 0.137 EPA/dropback (8th), -0.076 EPA/run (22nd) Defense: 17.2 points/game (1st), 285.9 yards/game (6th), 25 takeaways (6th), -0.113 EPA/play (1st), -0.065 EPA/dropback (5th), -0.206 EPA/run (1st) Even though it was ranked only 14th in the NFL in expected points added and turned the ball over more than every team but one during the 2025 regular season, the Seahawks offense was quite successful as a whole. That was particularly true in the passing game, where the team finished second in net yards per attempt (7.6) — a ranking mirrored by the defense (5.1). The points and yards per game rankings were impressive as well, but do not quite hold up when looked at on a drive-by-drive basis: Seattle was ranked 11th in both categories on a per-series average. Defensively, there was no such drop-off between the raw data and the efficiency metrics. Seattle finished the regular season first in points allowed per game (17.2) and first in points allowed per drive (1.48), sixth in yards per game (285.9) and fourth in yards per drive (25.8), and top-10 in virtually all major categories including scoring percentage (28.7%; 2nd) and turnover rate (12.8%; 6th). The run defense was particularly stout, but teams did not have any easier of a time moving the ball through the air. Long story short, this was as complete a defense as any in the NFL — and the Patriots found this out first-hand in the Super Bowl. Seahawks 2025 season In this section, we typically look back at the games already played this season. With this being opening week, however, there are no such points of reference. Instead, let’s recap Seattle’s championship campaign from a year ago. Week 1: 17-13 loss vs. San Francisco 49ers (0-1) Week 2: 31-17 win at Pittsburgh Steelers (1-1) Week 3: 44-13 win vs. New Orleans Saints (2-1) Week 4: 23-20 win at Arizona Cardinals (3-1) Week 5: 38-35 loss vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-2) Week 6: 20-12 win at Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) Week 7: 27-19 win vs. Houston Texans (5-2) Week 8: Bye Week 9: 38-14 win at Washington Commanders (6-2) Week 10: 44-22 win vs. Arizona Cardinals (7-2) Week 11: 21-19 loss at Los Angeles Rams (7-3) Week 12: 30-24 win at Tennessee Titans (8-3) Week 13: 26-0 win vs. Minnesota Vikings (9-3) Week 14: 37-9 win at Atlanta Falcons (10-3) Week 15: 18-16 win vs. Indianapolis Colts (11-3) Week 16: 38-37 (OT) win vs. Los Angeles Rams (12-3) Week 17: 27-10 win vs. Carolina Panthers (13-3) Week 18: 13-3 win at San Francisco 49ers (14-3) Wild card round: Bye Divisional round: 41-6 win vs. San Francisco 49ers NFC Championship Game: 31-27 win vs. Los Angeles Rams Super Bowl: 29-13 win vs. New England Patriots All things considered, the Seahawks were deserving world champions last season. They were arguably the strongest team already in the regular season, posting a league-best scoring differential of +191, before going on a dominant postseason run. Seahawks active roster Roster up-to-date as of Sept. 7, 7 a.m. ET | *denotes nominal starter Quarterback (3): Sam Darnold* (14), Drew Lock (2), Jalen Milroe (6) Running back (4): Jadarian Price* (8), George Holani (36), Emanuel Wilson (23), Brady Russell (38 | FB) Wide receiver (5): Jaxon Smith-Njigba* (11), Cooper Kupp* (10), Rashid Shaheed* (22 | KR/PR), Torry Horton (15), Montorie Foster Jr. (87) Tight end (4): A.J. Barner* (88), Eric Saubert (81), Elijah Arroyo (18), Nick Kallerup (89) Offensive tackle (3): Charles Cross* (67 | LT), Abraham Lucas* (72 | RT), Josh Jones (74) Interior offensive line (6): Grey Zabel* (76 | LG), Jalen Sundell* (61 | C), Anthony Bradford* (75 | RG), Olusegun Oluwatimi (55), Beau Stephens (70), Christian Haynes (64), Bryce Cabeldue (77) Interior defensive line (6): Leonard Williams* (99), Byron Murphy II* (91), Jarran Reed (90), Brandon Pili (95), Mike Morris (94), Rylie Mills (98) Defensive edge (5): DeMarcus Lawrence* (0), Uchenna Nwosu* (7), Derrick Hall (58), Dante. Fowler Jr. (56), Connor O’Toole (57) Linebacker (5): Ernest Jones IV* (13), Drake Thomas* (42), Tyrice Knight (48), Patrick O’Connell (52), Chazz Surratt (44) Cornerback (4): Devon Witherspoon* (21), Josh Jobe* (29), Nehemiah Pritchett (28), Julian Neal (1) Safety (4): Nick Emmanwori* (3), Julian Love* (20), Ty Okada* (39), Avery Smith (27) Specialists (3): Jason Myers (5 | K), Michael Dickson (4 | P/H), Chris Stoll (41 | LS) Long gone are the days when Sam Darnold was the latest in a long list of quarterbacks failing to live up to the expectation of being a highly-drafted quarterback with the New York Jets. The journey to Seattle was not an easy one to travel for the third overall pick in the 2018 NFL Draft, but he made it count and is coming off the best season of his career: Darnold was the motor powering one of the league’s top offenses in 2025, and there is no reason to believe in a serious drop-off even under a new offensive coordinator. Of course, it helps when you have one of the best wide receiver trios in football to throw to. The first player to mention is, of course, JSN. The reigning NFL Offensive Player of the Year, Jaxon Smith-Njigba finished the 2025 regular season with 119 catches for a league-leading 1,793 yards and 10 touchdowns. Darnold’s go-to guy and big-play threat all rolled into one, he added 17 passes for 199 yards and a pair of scores in the playoffs. In 20 total games last season, the first-team All-Pro cracked 100 receiving yards 10 times. One prominent departure from last year, meanwhile, is running back Kenneth Walker. The MVP of Super Bowl LX signed with the Chiefs this offseason, and was replaced by Jadarian Price in the first round of the draft. Price will be running behind a high-quality offensive line that retained all five starters this offseason. On the other side of the ball, the Seahawks are featuring one of the most disruptive defensive lines in football. Led by a starting quartet of edge rushers DeMarcus Lawrence and Uchenna Nwosu as well as interior linemen Leonard Williams and Byron Murphy, blocking Seattle’s front line again projects to be a handful for opposing offenses. The Patriots, of course, were unable to limit the group’s impact in the Super Bowl. The hope is that some reshuffling as well as some natural growth from youngsters Will Campbell and Jared Wilson will make for a more competitive battle this time…

title: Examining the roster ties between Patriots, Seahawks ahead of Week 1
summary: Familiarity from February remains heading into the first game of September. Between the active rosters, practice squads and reserve lists, four players in the fold for the 2026 season opener have been both New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks during their NFL journeys. Here’s a glance through those connections ahead of Wednesday’s 8:20 p.m. ET […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 22: Dre'Mont Jones #5 of the New England Patriots reacts against the Philadelphia Eagles during an NFL preseason football game at Gillette Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Familiarity from February remains heading into the first game of September. Between the active rosters, practice squads and reserve lists, four players in the fold for the 2026 season opener have been both New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks during their NFL journeys. Here’s a glance through those connections ahead of Wednesday’s 8:20 p.m. ET Super Bowl LX rematch at Lumen Field. SEATTLE Eric Saubert, tight end — Saubert has been a member of 11 organizations since becoming Drake University’s first NFL draft choice in 34 years. The No. 174 overall selection in the 2017 class spent his initial campaigns with the Atlanta Falcons before being acquired at Gillette Stadium in exchange for a conditional pick back in 2019. The stint started and finished that August at the league’s 53-man roster deadline. But the 32-year-old blocking tight end has found a home with the Super Bowl LX champions on the heels of myriad transactions. Saubert signed a one-year deal with Seattle in 2025 and had earned a one-year extension after activated from injured reserve last December. A veteran of 112 games in the regular season, including 24 starts, he has caught 51 passes for 420 yards and three touchdowns. An additional two starts came during the Seahawks’ latest playoff run. NEW ENGLAND Ben Brown, guard — The Patriots released Brown as the NFL deadline dust settled last week. The vested veteran, who signed a contract extension in December, quickly returned to the 53-man roster after the procedural move. Brown’s NFL career got underway as an undrafted free agent with the Cincinnati Bengals in 2022. A torn biceps in his preseason debut resulted in him spending all of his rookie season on injured reserve. Waived the following August, the Ole Miss product signed to the Seattle practice squad. From there, Brown was promoted to the active roster that September, waived and re-signed to the practice squad that October, then let go that November. Stints with the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders followed before he was signed off the latter’s practice squad and started at center in Foxborough the same week in the fall off 2024. The 28-year-old interior lineman has gone on to appear in 27 games for New England, starting 14 between center and guard while totaling 998 snaps on offense and 124 snaps on special teams. Greg Van Roten, guard — A veteran of 144 NFL games toured Foxborough in August. And as injuries mounted along the offensive line in the preseason, that visit that gave way to a contract. The 36-year-old Van Roten had been unsigned since opening of the new league year. He now resides on the reigning AFC champions’ 53-man roster. Standing 105 starts into his run, the 2012 undrafted free agent out of Penn has also been a member of the Green Bay Packers, Jacksonville Jaguars, New York Jets and Buffalo Bills. And in 2014, Van Roten spent six months in Seattle before being released at the 53-man roster deadline and moving into the CFL ranks with the Toronto Argonauts. Between guard and center, the veteran has amassed 105 starts and finished past two campaigns having logged 100 percent of the offensive snaps. Dre’Mont Jones, outside linebacker — The Patriots reached a three-year deal with Jones as the official start of NFL free agency loomed in March. The 29-year-old edge rusher and convert from defensive tackle checks in as a veteran of 108 games and 69 starts. Entering the league out of Ohio State in the third round of the 2019 draft at No. 71 overall, Jones has since racked up 253 tackles, 37.5 sacks, three forced fumbles, three fumble recoveries and one interception. He spent 2025 between the Tennessee Titans and Baltimore Ravens by way of trade. Prior to then, Jones saw action in every game across a pair of campaigns with Seattle before being released entering the final leg of a three-year contract. His Seahawks stay featured 23 starts, 8.5 sacks as well as a safety.

title: If the Saints win/lose vs. Lions
summary: The regular season is finally upon us, and the New Orleans Saints are set to open their 2026 campaign on the road against the Detroit Lions. Here’s a preview of what either result could mean for the black and gold on Sunday. If the Saints win: Should the Saints go into Detroit on Sunday afternoon […]
full_text: The regular season is finally upon us, and the New Orleans Saints are set to open their 2026 campaign on the road against the Detroit Lions. Here’s a preview of what either result could mean for the black and gold on Sunday. If the Saints win: Should the Saints go into Detroit on Sunday afternoon and win the game, it would likely be in contention as one of the biggest surprises of the week across the NFL. It would amplify the hype that’s been building all offseason since the Saints finished last year on such a strong note, and make for a real statement of intent for the campaign ahead. With a trip to Baltimore on the horizon next week, a victory would do wonders for New Orleans with such a tough pair of games to open the season. Such an outcome would require the team to make big plays on both sides of the ball, forcing turnovers while limiting their own. It’s the sort of win that instantly raises the expectations of outside observers and would set the tone in emphatic fashion. If the Saints lose: A loss in Detroit shouldn’t cause any panic or despondency. Of course, the manner in which the defeat arrives can have a huge bearing on the conclusions one might draw; the Saints shouldn’t get blown out here. But a defeat on the road against a team with aspirations of a deep playoff run is indeed the likelier outcome. Regardless, Kellen Moore will want to see signs that his team is trending in the right direction, and that can be the case even in defeat. Can the Saints pull off the upset to start the season 1-0? How high are your expectations for the year? Let us know in the comments!

title: Mike Detillier: More Than a Voice on the Radio
summary: Some losses hit differently. The news that Mike Detillier had died Sunday was one of those moments. A native of Lafourche Parish, Mike began his career in engineering before becoming one of the most trusted and recognizable voices in Louisiana sports. He first gained widespread recognition through Mike Detillier’s NFL Draft Report, which he launched […]
full_text: Some losses hit differently. The news that Mike Detillier had died Sunday was one of those moments. A native of Lafourche Parish, Mike began his career in engineering before becoming one of the most trusted and recognizable voices in Louisiana sports. He first gained widespread recognition through Mike Detillier’s NFL Draft Report, which he launched in 1985 and developed into a respected resource for football fans. His knowledge and passion for the game soon took him to the airwaves, where he became a familiar voice on Sports Talk during Buddy Diliberto’s tenure. Those appearances eventually led to a longtime role with WWL, where Mike shared his insight and expertise as a college and professional football analyst. But for all of his knowledge of the game, it was his genuine love for people and his willingness to share that knowledge that made Mike so special. He wasn’t simply a football analyst. He was a mentor, a teacher, a sounding board and, most importantly, a friend. Mike was only 65, far too young, and his death leaves a tremendous void in Louisiana’s sports media community. For decades, his voice was part of the soundtrack of sports in this state, heard regularly on WWL. But to those of us who had the privilege of knowing Mike beyond the microphone, he was so much more than a sports media personality. Long before I had the opportunity to know Mike personally, I was one of the many people who listened to him talk football. His voice had been familiar to me for years, long before I ever walked into the Saints facility. So, when I started covering the Saints and had the opportunity to get to know Mike, I never took it for granted. Someone I had listened to and respected for years became someone I could turn to for advice, encouragement and perspective. And despite all of his experience and success, Mike welcomed me from Day 1, treated me like a colleague and was always willing to help. He was incredibly kind and generous with his time, never hesitating to answer a question, offer advice or share what he knew. He never treated me like the rookie trying to find her way. He treated me like an equal. That meant more to me than he probably ever realized. Over the years, Mike became much more than someone I could turn to for advice about sports or journalism. He became someone I was incredibly proud to call a friend. That was the thing about Mike. He cared about people. He cared about the business he was part of, but he cared just as much about the people trying to find their way in it. He understood that success wasn’t just about getting the next story or landing the next interview. It was about building relationships, earning trust and helping the people around you along the way. Mike did that naturally. He had a way of making you feel comfortable, whether you had known him for years or had just met him. He was a wealth of knowledge and could talk sports with just about anyone, but his greatest gift was making people feel like they mattered. His death is especially heartbreaking because it all happened so quickly. Mike had only recently learned that he had Stage 4 metastatic pancreatic cancer after being rushed to the hospital with stomach pain. He had not yet had the opportunity to share the devastating news publicly. In fact, Mike was planning to tell his WWL audience about his diagnosis after Labor Day, on what would have been his 66th birthday. There wasn’t enough time. Not enough time for more conversations. Not enough time for more stories. Not enough time for more laughs, more advice or another opportunity to simply say thank you. He never got the chance to tell his listeners himself. That makes his sudden passing even harder to comprehend. Former Saints quarterback Bobby Hebert, who worked alongside Mike at WWL, perhaps put it best. “Mike was a good friend and was like a brother to me. It’s heartbreaking. This really hurts.” It does. For so many Louisiana sports fans, Mike’s voice was part of their lives. For those of us fortunate enough to know him personally, his impact went far beyond what people heard on the radio. I will always be grateful for the conversations, the lessons, the encouragement and the kindness Mike showed me throughout the years. Those are the things you remember. Those are the things that last. The sports world will continue. The games will be played. The shows will go on. Another story will always be waiting to be written. But there will be an empty chair, a missing voice and countless people who will think of Mike when they sit down to talk sports. I know I’ll be one of them. Mike Detillier was a beloved voice in Louisiana sports, a respected media personality and one of the most knowledgeable people I’ve ever known in this business. But to so many of us, he was something even more important. He was simply Mike — a friend. And I feel incredibly lucky to have known him.

title: Saints enter 2026 NFL season with second-easiest strength of schedule
summary: The New Orleans Saints are set to enter the 2026 NFL season with one of the easiest schedules. Saints’ opponents for 2026 had a win percentage of .434 in 2025, just .005 better than the Cleveland Browns’ opponents, who had a win percentage of .429. New Orleans finished last in the NFC South in 2025 […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - DECEMBER 28: Head Coach Kellen Moore congratulates Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints on the sidelines after a touchdown during a game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Nashville, Tennessee. The Saints defeated the Titans 34-26. (Photo by Wesley Hitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are set to enter the 2026 NFL season with one of the easiest schedules. Saints’ opponents for 2026 had a win percentage of .434 in 2025, just .005 better than the Cleveland Browns’ opponents, who had a win percentage of .429. Each team's strength of schedule this season 📊 pic.twitter.com/4ozyTPKI8N — NFL (@NFL) September 6, 2026 New Orleans finished last in the NFC South in 2025 with a 6-11 record. With their division placement, the Saints are awarded a 4th-place schedule, matching them up with other 4th-place finishers. The Saints will face the Arizona Cardinals, Las Vegas Raiders, New York Giants, and their Week 1 opponent, the Detroit Lions, thanks to finishing last in the division. Also factoring into their weak strength of schedule is the lack of power in the NFC South. Each of the Saints’ division rivals finished 8-9 in 2025. While the black and gold finished last in 2025, there are expectations that they will place better in 2026 with an improved roster and questions among their rivals. Outside the Carolina Panthers, who finished first in 2025, the entire NFC South has a strength-of-schedule rating under .500. Despite this, Carolina is the favorite to win the division in 2026. The Atlanta Falcons are expected to take a step back, and there are plenty of questions surrounding the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. While New Orleans has the quote-unquote easiest schedule in the NFC South, their schedule isn’t as easy as it seems. The Lions are a better team than they finished last season, and they’ll follow that tough Week 1 matchup with a tough road trip to the Baltimore Ravens. While an easier strength of schedule should result in more wins for the Saints in 2026, it’s still the NFL. Any team can win on any given Sunday, and that’s true for New Orleans, who are projected to enter as underdogs for a majority of their matchups for the upcoming season. The plan should be simple. Go in every week and give it your all, no matter the opponent.

Considering what we’ve seen from Shough this offseason, whether it be his work ethic or him consistently building chemistry with his teammates, New Orleans should expect him to play with more confidence and take advantage of opportunities when they present themselves. More importantly, it could reinforce the belief that the production he showed toward the end of last season wasn’t a fluke. Shough doesn’t need to be perfect. title: Darius Slayton cut is a gamble the NY Giants might regret
summary: John Harbaugh is running a meritocracy, and Darius Slayton’s play this summer did not warrant him being ahead of any other wide receiver on the New York Giants’ roster. That is the biggest reason Slayton is an ex-Giant today. Slayton missed the entire spring after double sports hernia surgery. He had a quiet summer, admitting […]
full_text: Darius Slayton | Getty Images John Harbaugh is running a meritocracy, and Darius Slayton’s play this summer did not warrant him being ahead of any other wide receiver on the New York Giants’ roster. That is the biggest reason Slayton is an ex-Giant today. Slayton missed the entire spring after double sports hernia surgery. He had a quiet summer, admitting not long ago that he still was not running at 100%, though he felt “pretty good.” Malik Nabers is the Giants’ No. 1 wide receiver. Malachi Fields, Odell Beckham Jr., and Darnell Mooney were all better than Slayton this summer. For that matter, practice squad receivers Braxton Berrios and Dalen Cambre were also better. Slayton was ticketed for the game-day inactive list when Sunday’s season-opening game against the Dallas Cowboys rolled around. None of that means that cutting Slayton isn’t a massive gamble by the Giants. The Giants have already lost one wide receiver they were going to count on heavily, Calvin Austin, to a season-ending injury. Depth at the position is now, to use an informal word, sketchy. Yes, moving on from Slayton is likely a sign that the Giants feel good about the possibility that Nabers will play Sunday against the Cowboys. Even if he plays, though, Nabers will probably play a limited number of snaps in his return from last season’s torn ACL. Fields is a rookie third-round pick. He had an impressive summer, but there is no guarantee he can carry that performance into real games. We have seen impressive summers fizzle before when fall arrived. Beckham earned his spot, no doubt. Still, he is a 33-year-old who did not play in 2025 and has not played a full NFL season since 2019 — yes, 2019. How much can he play? How long before his body breaks down and he misses time? How productive can he be when he does play? Darnell Mooney has a 1,000-yard and a 900-yard receiving season on his resume over six NFL seasons. He is coming off a down year with the Atlanta Falcons, though, where he caught just 32 passes for 443 yards. Are the Giants going to get a version of Mooney that deserves consistent playing time? What about the practice squad guys? Berrios has six receptions in 10 games over the past two seasons. Cambre was impressive this summer, but he has played 16 NFL offensive snaps and does not have a catch. Jalin Hyatt? Thirteen receptions over the past two seasons. Charlie Jones has eight catches in 33 career games, only one of which came in the last two seasons. Can any of them produce at an acceptable level if the Giants need them to play extended snaps at wide receiver? That is debatable. Slayton hate is unwarranted The subhead says exactly what it is meant to say. Slayton has been a better player than many Giants fans, needing someone or something to blame for the struggles of recent seasons, are willing to admit. Yes, his career drop rate of 6.3% is too high. No, he was never able to be what the Giants needed in the pre-Nabers days — a bona fide No. 1 receiver. Let’s be real, though. Slayton was a fifth-round pick, 171st overall, out of Auburn in the 2019 NFL Draft. He has not been an All-Pro like 2023 fifth-round pick Puka Nacua, but Slayton has vastly outplayed his draft position. Slayton led the Giants in receiving yards four times in seven seasons, with 700+ receiving yards in each of those seasons. He has a 15.0 yards-per-catch average. He is four catches shy of 300 for his career, and his 4,435 receiving yards are 565 short of 5,000. Slayton is 14th on the team’s all-time receptions list. His career average is 42 receptions per season. If he accomplished that in 2026, he would have moved all the way to ninth. Slayton is 12th on the team’s all-time list in receiving yards. His average 633-yard receiving season would have skyrocketed him to fifth, behind only Amani Toomer, Odell Beckham Jr., Frank Gifford, and Tiki Barber. Slayton has been a good player for the Giants. Instead of ripping him for his shortcomings and pointing a finger at him as part of the reason the team has been mostly awful during his time in New York, fans should be thanking him for being an overachiever, a good player, and an excellent representative of the franchise during his time with it. We have seen Slayton outplay expectations before. There might come a time this season when the Giants wish they still had him around to try and do it again.

title: NY Giants release WR Darius Slayton, team’s longest-tenured player
summary: The New York Giants announced Tuesday afternoon that they have released veteran wide receiver Darius Slayton. Slayton, 29, was drafted by the Giants in the fifth round of the 2019 NFL Draft and was, up until his release, the longest-tenured Giant on the roster. The Giants create just $3.16 million in cap space while taking […]
full_text: Darius Slayton | Getty Images The New York Giants announced Tuesday afternoon that they have released veteran wide receiver Darius Slayton . Slayton, 29, was drafted by the Giants in the fifth round of the 2019 NFL Draft and was, up until his release, the longest-tenured Giant on the roster. The Giants create just $3.16 million in cap space while taking on $12.75 million in dead cap money by releasing Slayton. Slayton made an immediate impact for the Giants as a rookie. His uncommon blend of size and speed made him a much-needed deep threat, and he quickly built a strong rapport with fellow 2019 draftee, quarterback Daniel Jones. While Slayton never cracked 800 yards receiving, he did eclipse 700 yards in four of his first five seasons (2019, 2020, 2022, and 2023). He led the Giants in receiving in each of those seasons. Slayton quickly took to social media after his release. Grateful for my time in NY. 7 years a Giant nothing but love for one of the most prestigious organizations in the NFL. Excited to see what’s next 🙏🏾 — Darius Slayton (@Young_Slay2) September 7, 2026 That said, while Slayton provided a much-needed vertical element to the Giants’ offense, he has struggled to consistently generate separation with his route running. He has also struggled with drops throughout his career. Slayton played in 106 games for the Giants, starting 78. He has 296 catches for 4,435 yards and 22 touchdowns as a Giant. Despite his limitations, Slayton was an undeniable hit as a fifth-round pick. Slayton had double sports hernia surgery in the offseason, and recently admitted that he still did not feel he was running as well as he could. The release of Slayton positions Darnell Mooney and rookie Malachi Fields to be primary receivers along with Malik Nabers and Odell Beckham Jr. It remains to be seen how the Giants will fill the roster hole created by releasing Slayton. They could sign Braxton Berrios to their active roster, or they could add a free agent and keep their trio of returners on the practice squad. The Giants also have wide receivers Dalen Cambre , Jalin Hyatt , and newly-signed Charlie Jones on the practice squad.

title: ESPN projects a 7-win season for the Giants
summary: How will the 2026 season play out? Well, nobody really knows. That, of course, isn’t stopping people from trying to project it. Seth Walder of ESPN released their prediction of how the season will go on Monday. ESPN’s projections are based on their football power index (FPI) and 10,000 simulations of the season. The average […]
full_text: The New York Giants take the field. | Getty Images How will the 2026 season play out? Well, nobody really knows. That, of course, isn’t stopping people from trying to project it. Seth Walder of ESPN released their prediction of how the season will go on Monday . ESPN’s projections are based on their football power index (FPI) and 10,000 simulations of the season. The average result of those simulations has the New York Giants finishing with a 7-10 record amid season-ending losses to the Cowboys and Eagles. With two weeks left, the Cowboys, Eagles and Giants were in a three-way tie with mediocre 7-8 records. It took weeks for Philadelphia to find its offensive rhythm under new coordinator Sean Mannion. The Cowboys’ new-look defense held up well early in the season but couldn’t sustain that improvement, causing Dallas to enter the final two weeks on a four-game losing streak. The Giants’ passing game struggled early with wide receiver Malik Nabers being limited but got better as he got healthier. All three teams had a shot at the playoffs with two games left. The Cowboys dealt a major blow to New York in Week 17, winning a 19-7 defensive battle. The Eagles upset the 49ers 23-19 on the road. But the Cowboys had the tiebreaker advantage, so Dallas took the division when it beat the Commanders in Week 18 even though Philadelphia prevailed over the Giants to finish with an identical 9-8 record. The playoffs start off with a bang for the Cowboys, with Dak Prescott putting up 31 points on the Seahawks’ defense, while limiting Seattle to just 19. They come crashing back to Earth the next week and are ejected from the dance by the Detroit Lions. Chris’ thoughts Could this scenario come to pass? Well, obviously, anything can happen. However I think I’d be pretty stunned if this exact scenario played out — and probably nowhere near as stunned as the folks at ESPN would be if their prediction came true. I’m not surprised that ESPN’s models are pretty low on the NFC East. After all, the division was weak last year, and these models tend to be rear-looking. However, the division also abounds with new coordinators and schemes and nobody quite knows how the various units will perform under their new coaches. The Cowboys are widely expected to make a leap thanks to the arrival of new DC Christian Parker and rookie S Caleb Downs. However, Downs is in fact a rookie, and there’s always a learning curve with rookies. Likewise, while Parker is a Vic Fangio disicple and has been hailed as a wunderkind, he has never run an NFL defense before. There’s no way to definitively say whether he will be a success or not. Likewise, Sean Manion has never run an NFL offense and the Eagles will be without A.J. Brown. The Eagles have been more efficient and explosive with Green than without him, and we don’t know if Dontavian Wicks will be able to fill Brown’s shoes or how Jalen Hurts will adapt to his new reality. And finally, the Washington Commanders may be planning to ape Brian Flores’ blitz-happy approach to mask their defensive limitations. Will they? And if they do, will it work? And can Jayden Daniels stay healthy for the full season and return to his rookie form? The Giants, as we’ve covered extensively, have completely retooled their offense and defense. Nobody is quite surewhat the former will look like under Matt Nagy, Brian Callahan, and Greg Roman. It is interesting that the media is so high on rookie coaches like Parker and Manion, while dismissing the Giants’ own experienced coaching staff. I’ll admit my bias in being optimistic for the Giants this year. But (as I’ve written before) it seems odd to me that so many are predicting that the best the Giants can do is win the same number of games they should have won the year before. And with what is expected to be a stronger roster and far better coaching, at that. The good news is that we’ll get the answers to all these questions soon, as opening day is rapidly approaching. But for now, it’s still fun to speculate as we pass the time.

title: Jaxson Dart fails to crack Top 20 in The Athletic’s QBI metric
summary: New York Giants second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart ranks 21st in the NFL, at least per The Athletic’s new “QBI” metric. I should probably take a step back and explain what “QBI” is, and what it’s trying to do. Or rather, let the metric’s creator, Austin Mock, describe the stat. Mock explains, QBI is a metric […]
full_text: New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images New York Giants second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart ranks 21st in the NFL, at least per The Athletic’s new “QBI” metric . I should probably take a step back and explain what “QBI” is, and what it’s trying to do. Or rather, let the metric’s creator, Austin Mock, describe the stat. Mock explains, QBI is a metric we’ve created that strips away the contributions from a quarterback’s 10 offensive teammates and credits only what the quarterback provides on a per-play basis. QBI is a forward-looking quarterback efficiency metric that uses play-by-play data, adjusts for context in each play and is opponent-aware. Put more simply, QBI takes into account passes, rushes, scrambles, sacks, turnovers and anything else that happens when the football is in the quarterback’s hands. But it goes a step deeper and adjusts for whether the quarterback was pressured, if that pressure was quick (less than 2.5 seconds), as well as the quality of the offensive line and receivers. QBI factors in fumbles in an attempt to take the luck out of recoveries — this can work for and against a quarterback depending on who recovered. QBI also takes into account drops by receivers, as well as yards after the catch and uses an expected YAC model to assign or remove credit from the quarterback. Of course, EPA and success rate are factors in the model, as well. Mock adds that QBI also factors in PFF grades in an attempt to incorporate a film aspect. He also explains that he’s taken inspiration from baseball analytics (wRC+, to be specific) and normalized a ‘100’ QBI grade to be “average”. From there, he considers ‘101’ to be starter caliber play and ‘130’ to be “Pro Bowl” caliber play. Zooming back in to Jaxson Dart, the Giants’ QB is one of three quarterbacks to earn an even “100” grade for last year, along with Jalen Hurts of the Philadelphia Eagles and Jared Goff of the Detroit Lions. Dart is the second-highest graded rookie from last year’s class, trailing only Tyler Shough, who graded out as a 103. Dart’s 100 was good for 21st in the NFL, while Shough’s 103 ranks him 15th. That said, Dart also finished well ahead of Tennessee Titans’ QB Cam Ward (78) and Cleveland Browns QB Shedeur Sanders (47). We’ve already seen an interesting dynamic forming around Dart and Shough in the eyes of the NFL. Dart led the rookie QBs in The Athletic’s annual Quarterback Tiers ranking at 24th, just edging out Ward (25th) and Shough (t-26th). However, they noted that defensive coaches respect Dart significantly more than the offensive coaches and executives, who prefer Shough. That is largely due to the fact that Dart had a significantly more volatile game in 2025 than did Shough. So while Dart was more apt to thrive in chaos or create huge plays, Shough was more willing to play within the structure of the offense and be efficient on a down-to-down basis. That’s likely reflected in Shough’s higher QBI score, as there are fewer negative plays to bring the score down. However, Mock also points out that we shouldn’t read too much into QBI scores when projecting the rookies to their second seasons. There’s more background to my methodology, but one interesting note is that when testing out QBI’s projective capabilities, I found it was beneficial to shrink the impact of a quarterback’s rookie season. Suffice it to say, a QB’s rookie year is not always an accurate portrayal of the player that QB will become. For a young QB, their projections might seem regressed to the mean, and that’s on purpose. I’ve written before that perhaps the biggest unlock for Dart is to become better at operating within the structure of the offense. I believe that starts with improving his footwork and using that to marry his eyes and progression with the rhythm of the offense. If Dart can consistently work within the structure of the Giants’ offense while also understanding when to break out and play sandlot football, we could see him make a real leap in his second year. We’ve gotten reports that Dart improved significantly in that regard as the Giants have installed and refined their offense around him over the course of training camp. So perhaps that process has already begun. Mock adds that QBI will be used in a weekly quarterback ranking, so we’ll get an idea of how Dart compares to the other starters in the NFL — particularly once the small sample size volatility dies down. As Mock himself admits, there’s no one stat that perfectly captures quarterback play, or the play at any position for that matter. But this could be a useful tool to help us contextualize Dart’s performance and (hopefully) improvement over the course of the 2026 season.

title: Questions, Questions Everywhere
summary: A new season is about to get underway for the New York Jets, and with it come questions. Every season brings new questions, but this season just feels different in the magnitude of uncertainty surrounding the team. Some years, like in the 2010 season, the Jets had established veterans at most key positions. The talent […]
full_text: FLORHAM PARK, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 11: Geno Smith #7 of the New York Jets with Aaron Glenn head coach of the New York Jets during a joint practice between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and New York Jets at Atlantic Health Jets Training Center on August 11, 2026 in Florham Park, New Jersey. (Photo by Adam Hunger/Getty Images) | Getty Images A new season is about to get underway for the New York Jets, and with it come questions. Every season brings new questions, but this season just feels different in the magnitude of uncertainty surrounding the team. Some years, like in the 2010 season, the Jets had established veterans at most key positions. The talent was in place, the coaching was sound, at least on the defense, and we knew going in this was a team that, barring catastrophic injuries, was built to compete at the highest levels. Other seasons, like many of the last 15 years, the talent level was very low, the coaching was abysmal, and we knew going in that the team had very little chance to succeed. This year feels different. There seem to be questions at almost every level of the organization. Uncertainty seems extremely high. If most of the major questions are resolved to the upside, this could be an interesting and competitive team. If most of the major questions are resolved to the downside, this could be another season where the Jets are vying for one of the top spots in the upcoming NFL draft. Let’s take a look at some of the most pressing questions facing the Jets. Coaching It all starts at the top. Head coach Aaron Glenn had a concerning year in 2025, his first as an NFL head coach. Coming into the season cocky and adversarial with all who dared question him, Glenn was soon humbled by a team that ended up in the conversation for worst team in the NFL. When the trade deadline approached it was clear the team was really, really bad, and the Jets threw in the towel on the 2025 season by trading their two best players on defense, Quinnen Williams and Sauce Gardner. At that point, the defense utterly collapsed, putting forth one noncompetitive performance after another. A large part of this was clearly a lack of talent, but the coaching can’t completely escape blame. Once the season was over Glenn massively overhauled the coaching staff, bringing in new coaches at every level, including replacing the offensive and defensive coordinators.It is a bit odd for a head coach to need to fire nearly every coach he handpicked himself just a year earlier. Now Glenn may be on the hotseat. He likely will not survive another disastrous season. Can Glenn learn from his many mistakes of 2025? Will his new coaching staff prove to be more competent than last year’s crew? Is defensive playcalling really a Glenn superpower? Will the Jets look better prepared? Will they at times look like they have outcoached the opposition? Will they be better tacklers? Will the young players successfully develop? The head coach is a big part of any team’s success. Glenn did not look the part of a top head coach last season. Heck, he didn’t look the part of a competent head coach last season. How he learns from his mistakes and grows as a head coach will go a long way to determining the level of success or failure the Jets achieve this year. OFFENSE Quarterback Last season the Jets had an atrocious Justin Fields, a washed up Tyrod Taylor, and a practice squad level Brady Cook share the quarterback position. It did not go well. All three of those guys are now gone. In their place the Jets have acquired veteran Geno Smith via trade and rookie Cade Klubnik in the draft. Klubnik is probably not ready to play extensive snaps this season. That puts it all on Geno Smith. Geno Smith enjoyed a modicum of success with the Seattle Seahawks from 2022 through 2024 before the Seahawks decided to move on after the 2024 season. Former Seahawks head coach latched on with the Las Vegas Raiders, and he brought Geno Smith with him as the new Raiders starting quarterback. It did not go well. In 2025 Geno Smith started 15 games for the Raiders and led them to a 2-13 record in those games. He led the NFL in sacks and interceptions, an unfortunate duo of leading stats for Smith. Smith posted just 3025 passing yards and a career low 34 QBR. It was a bad performance for Smith, but there were pretty significant mitigating factors. Smith played behind arguably the worst offensive line in the NFL. His leading receivers were Brock Bowers, who was hobbled by injuries much of the season, Jakobi Meyers, who was traded after just seven games, and Tre Tucker. This was a terrible offensive environment. Any quarterback would have struggled. One season prior Smith led the Seahawks to a 10 – 7 record while passing for more than 4300 yards. The question now becomes, what can Smith produce for the Jets? Certainly the Jets will provide Smith a significantly better offensive line. Barring significant injuries the Jets should also provide Smith with better weapons. Unless the Jets suffer a rash of major injuries Smith should be better in 2026, but how much better? Smith will turn 36 years old this October. Age related decline is likely already taking place. Smith’s QBR has declined in each of the last three years. At this point Smith’s ceiling is likely something like a league average starting quarterback, which would be a major improvement on the dreck the Jets have been trotting out there in recent years. The question is, what is the floor? The answer will go a long way to determining the Jets’ fate in 2026. Offensive Line The offensive line has relatively few questions, a refreshing change from the recent past. Center Josh Myers is subpar, and new guard Dylan Parham is coming off a down year after a pretty good 2024. Will Parham rebound? Guard Joe Tippman is better than average and still improving. The two tackles, Armand Membou and Olu Fashanu, are young, ascending and talented. The depth isn’t great, but that is a league wide problem at offensive line. Bottom line, this is likely to be at least a league average unit with potential to develop into much better than average. Provided they avoid too many injuries, if the Jets offense fails, it is unlikely the offensive line will be a significant culprit. Running Backs Like the offensive line, this is a young and solid unit. Starter Breece Hall is a borderline top ten back. The perennially overlooked Isaiah Davis has quietly produced excellent play as Hall’s backup. He may be capable of more. Braelon Allen is the primary question here. Touted as a talented power back when he was drafted two years ago, Allen has failed to impress in his two years in the NFL. Now in his third year and coming into camp bigger and stronger than ever, this feels like a make or break season for Allen. Can he live up to prior expectations and develop into one of the better power backs in the NFL? If he does the Jets might have a running game that goes a long way towards taking the pressure off Geno Smith. Wide Receivers As usual, this group boils down to Garrett Wilson and a whole lot of questions. What seems different this year is the upside appears significantly greater. Adonai Mitchell has been unable to put it all together since he was drafted two years ago. He was buried on the Indianapolis Colts depth chart to start his career, then came over to the Jets in the Sauce Gardner trade last year. With Garrett Wilson sidelined by injury, Adonail Mitchell became the de facto WR1 for the Jets the rest of the season, and he did not thrive in that role. In eight games with the Jets Mitchell produced just two games with more than three receptions and just two games with more than 43 receiving yards. He caught just 41% of his targets, produced an abysmal 5.2 yards per target, and his quarterbacks had an unholy 41 passer rating throwing to Mitchell. Those are frighteningly bad numbers for a wide receiver, but there was one huge mitigating factor. The starting quarterbacks for Mitchell were the…

full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - NOVEMBER 30: Nick Folk #6 of the New York Jets kicks a field goal during the fourth quarter against the Atlanta Falcons at MetLife Stadium on November 30, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Kickers Cairo Santos, Bears Santos is one of a handful of former Jets kickers who ultimately settled with a team and established himself with them. He returns to Chicago, who he has now been with since 2020. Chase McLaughlin, Bucs Similarly, McLaughlin is well established in Tampa Bay and is returning for a fourth season with the Bucs. Jason Myers, Seahawks Myers remains in Seattle, where he has been since he left the Jets following a pro bowl season in 2018. Nick Folk, Falcons Speaking of Jets who left immediately after a great season, Folk signed with Atlanta and will be their kicker in 2026. Spencer Shrader, Colts Shrader won the Colts’ job last year but missed most of the season due to injury and their kicker down the stretch was Blake Grupe. Grupe is, of course, now with the Jets, after Shrader won their competition. Riley Patterson, Dolphins Jason Sanders is now on the Jets’ practice squad after spending all of last year on injured reserve while another ex-Jet held onto his old job. Patterson has been retained for this year, while Sanders failed to win the Jets’ role. Eddy Pineiro, 49ers Pineiro had three solid years with the Panthers after leaving the Jets but moved to San Francisco last season and they opted to bring him back with no competition. Harrison Mevis, Rams Mevis won the Rams job after doing well there at the end of last season. That makes a quarter of the league that currently has an ex-Jet as their placekicker. Lenny Krieg, Packers Krieg didn’t last very long in the competition for the Packers’ job but they opted to keep him on the practice squad as their International Pathway Player. Punters Braden Mann, Eagles Mann has also found a permanent home for himself after moving on from the Jets and is now entrenched as the Eagles’ punter. Kai Kroeger, Texans Kroeger was traded from the Saints to the Texans in the offseason and locked down their punter job with a solid preseason. Return Specialists Kalif Raymond, Bears Raymond has been one of the league’s most reliable punt returners for the Lions over the past several years, but he’ll be doing it in a different home this year, in Chicago. Malachi Corley, Browns Corley is also likely to play a significant role on special teams, as he did last season. He is listed as the Browns’ first string kickoff returner. Ty Johnson, Bills Johnson also regularly gets work as a kickoff returner and that’s likely to continue in 2026. Others The likes of Braxton Berrios, Brandon Codrington and Greg Dortch could all make contributions as returners this year but are currently on practice squads rather than active rosters. Other Special Teams Contributors Chargers linebacker Del’Shawn Phillips , who led the league with 24 special teams tackles, is one of the top special teams contributors in the NFL. Seattle’s Chazz Surratt and Zaire Barnes of the Giants are also productive in coverage, as is Carolina’s Claud Cherelus . Lions safety Chuck Clark also usually makes good contributions on special teams, as does Giants defensive back Elijah Campbell . As we know, Irv Charles is a top punt gunner, but he’s on Seattle’s injured reserve right now. Finally, Browns defensive tackle Shelby Harris , Commanders defensive tackle Javon Kinlaw and Leonard Taylor III of the Patriots have all shown a knack for blocking kicks.

title: Eagles News: NFL secondary rankings have Philadelphia in the top four
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Though there might be some volatility with Riq Woolen, the Eagles could very well have the NFL’s top cornerback trio. The depth at corner is a bit of a question mark. Michael Carter II could conceivably be a good backup nickel […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JUNE 10: Philadelphia Eagles cornerback Cooper DeJean #33 and Philadelphia Eagles cornerback Quinyon Mitchell #27 goof around during the Philadelphia Eagles off season minicamp on June 10th, 2026 at the Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! Though there might be some volatility with Riq Woolen, the Eagles could very well have the NFL’s top cornerback trio. The depth at corner is a bit of a question mark. Michael Carter II could conceivably be a good backup nickel option … and then the veteran Jonathan Jones has experience on both the outside and inside. The Eagles are weakest on defense at safety but I don’t think anyone needs to be panicking about that position. I think they’re going to be fine there. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … 2026 NFL secondary rankings: Patriots lead the way with a star-studded group – PFF 4) Philadelphia Eagles. This secondary had the highest collective PFF run-defense grade of any team last year, and Tariq Woolen now joins to establish one of the league’s strongest groups alongside Cooper DeJean and Quinyon Mitchell, who ranked second in completion percentage allowed behind Christian Gonzalez. By allowing Reed Blankenship to walk in free agency, Philadelphia has shed its largest liability from last season — his 42.8 PFF grade was the lowest of any Eagles starter. Can the Eagles’ Riq Woolen be Howie Roseman’s next one-year success story? – Inquirer Unlocking the “best version” of Woolen is no simple task. This offseason was a microcosm of his career — with peaks during OTAs, when he looked like the team’s best defender, and the valleys on Day 1 of the Eagles’ joint practice in New England, when A.J. Brown and the Patriots wide receiving corps torched him (before Woolen redeemed himself with a pair of interceptions on Day 2). Fangio perhaps put it best when asked about Woolen in early August. “At times he can get a little lazy or sloppy with his technique and have a bad down or two, but he’s still showing everything that I think he can do,” Fangio said. “He’s just got to get in such great shape and calloused to football that those don’t happen.” Graham has a different interpretation of Woolen’s work ethic — and believes that, under Fangio’s defense and direct coaching style, he’ll earn an even bigger contract next season. “I think that Riq makes stuff look so easy sometimes that you almost think it’s lazy — but it’s really not,” Graham said. “I know Vic coaches hard … but he’s probably Santa Claus compared to me. Because [Fangio’s] still talking to pros. I coached extremely hard. So I don’t think that type of stuff bothers him. But I think there is a next level … I think he’s a $15 to $20 million per year corner, long-term.” The Eagles will need a receiver to step up in 2026 – BGN The drop-off in receivers would be a bit less worrisome if the tight end situation was better. But after Goedert, who is now 31, there is absolutely nothing. Like Lemon, second round pick Eli Stowers was expected to come in and serve as a secondary pass catcher to Goedert. But Stowers’ summer has been brutal, appearing totally overmatched at this level. It is entirely possible he won’t even be activated on game days this year. That leaves the Eagles with run-blocking specialist Johnny Mundt and frequent practice squad player E.J. Jenkins as the back-ups. If Goedert goes down with an injury, something that happens almost every year, the tight end position will be totally and utterly useless in the passing game. The bottom line: someone outside of DeVonta Smith needs to step up this season. The Eagles need a receiver to emerge from this muddled pack to be Hurts’ reliable No. 2. They need a chain-mover, someone to pile up 700-800 yards this year and give opposing defenses someone else to think about other than Smith. Without it, I don’t see how this offense can function. NFC Hierarchy/Obituary: Week 1 edition – PhillyVoice 3) Eagles (11-6 in 2025): After having watched the Eagles practice all summer, I get asked quite a bit what I think of the team, in sort of a big picture way. And, well, they’re going to be a good team again. They have a high floor because the defense is going to be awesome. I’d be pretty stunned if they didn’t win double digit games again. The offense? I have no idea. There may not be a wider range of outcomes for one side of the ball in the NFL than this offensive group. We saw in 2024 how good they can be, and then in 2025 how bad they can be. I really don’t know. NFL team previews 2026: Predictions, rankings, depth charts – ESPN Bold prediction for 2026: Jonathan Greenard will record at least 0.8 sacks per game. I’m framing it that way because it’s unclear when Greenard will be back from a pec strain in the offseason. Once he’s on the field, I expect big things from Greenard playing alongside the rest of the defense, even after a down year in Minnesota. For context: 0.8 sacks per game translates to 13.6 sacks if he were to play all 17 games. Eagles superlatives: Jalen Carter for DPOY? Jalyx Hunt, Jihaad Campbell poised to break out – The Athletic Biggest concern — Wide receiver. The Eagles’ reconfigured wide receiver depth chart was hard to ascertain this summer with DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon missing three weeks of team drills. They need to avoid this looking like 2021, the season before A.J. Brown’s arrival. Smith showed clear upside that year, except the help around him kept the passing offense from reaching the level it needed. There’s a chance this all works as designed, with Smith looking like the bona fide No. 1 receiver, Wicks taking a leap with more opportunity in a familiar offense and Lemon showcasing the type of dynamic run-after-catch ability that made him such a threat at USC. Hollywood Brown and Elijah Moore offer experienced depth while Darius Cooper continues the development curve on display this summer. That’s the ideal scenario. Replacing Brown’s production in the aggregate makes sense on paper. It’s still possible they miss Brown more than fans might realize — and this looks like the season that compelled the Eagles to acquire Brown in the first place. DeVonta Smith taking control of Eagles’ new-look receiver room – NBCSP Aaron Moorehead had some pretty good advice for rookie receiver Makai Lemon about taking care of his body: “Whatever Smitty does, you do.” He probably didn’t even need to speak it. Because as DeVonta Smith enters his sixth NFL season in 2026, he is undoubtedly the guy in the Eagles’ new-look receiver room — the unquestioned WR1 after playing the last four seasons partially in the shadow of A.J. Brown. After months of speculation, the Eagles finally traded Brown to the Patriots back on June 1, which has allowed Smith to slide up into his new role as the Eagles’ top receiver. That is an important role on the field, but carries weight in the facility too. Moorehead said he challenged Smith this offseason to take over that role — “and he was ready for that.” “He’s not afraid to say something if it’s not right,” Moorehead said recently. “He’s kind of always been like that. I think that’s the Alabama (Nick) Saban in him. But I think even more so now, he’s able to take charge. He’s done a great job as far as leadership goes in the room, just helping everybody. That’s even Hollywood (Brown), who’s an older guy. It doesn’t matter. Adam Berry: From Wall Street to the Eagles’ front office – PhiladelphiaEagles.com After 14 years on Wall Street, Berry was officially hired as the Eagles’ director of football operations and strategy. Berry’s familiarity with numbers helped him transition into an NFL front office, working with the salary cap, contracts, and analytics. Roseman expected Berry to learn everything behind football operations, including college…
