title: NFL team previews 2026: Predictions, rankings, depth charts
summary: Here's everything you need to know for the 2026 regular season, including how all 32 NFL teams rank and key stats ahead of Week 1.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL season kicks off Wednesday with a Super Bowl rematch featuring the reigning champion  Seattle Seahawks hosting the New England Patriots  ( 8:20 p.m. ET, NBC ). Then, on Thursday, the NFL will have its first-ever regular-season game in Australia , where the Super Bowl-favorite  Los Angeles Rams will take on the San Francisco 49ers  ( 8:35 p.m. ET, Netflix ). 

 To welcome back football, we're previewing every single team in the league. Our NFL Nation reporters identified strengths and concerns for all 32 rosters, and then they laid out what would make 2026 a successful season. Analyst Matt Bowen gave a fantasy nugget for each team, analytics writer Seth Walder made 32 bold predictions, and ESPN Research provided QB stats to know.

 Plus, our Football Power Index predicted chances for every team to win its division, make the playoffs and more. The model even suggested best- and worst-case scenarios for all 32 teams, based on the 90th- and 10th-percentile outcomes across thousands of simulations, respectively.

 This is everything you need to know for the start of the season, which will conclude Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, for Super Bowl LXI on ESPN.

 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LV | LAC | LAR | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SEA 
 SF | TB | TEN | WSH 

 

 

 

 1. Los Angeles Rams 
 Chances to make the playoffs: 84.9% 
 Chances to win division: 50.4% 
 Projected wins: 11.3 
 Strength of schedule: Third hardest 
 2025 record: 12-5

 Biggest strength: The passing game. There are several options to choose from on this star-studded roster, but it's hard not to pick the reigning MVP. Quarterback Matthew Stafford is coming off the best season of his career and will again have one of the best receiver pairs in the NFL: Davante Adams and Puka Nacua . Last season, Adams led the league with 14 receiving touchdowns, and Nacua led the NFL with 129 catches. -- Sarah Barshop 

 Biggest concern: Offensive tackle. The Rams don't have much depth at tackle, which could matter if left tackle Alaric Jackson is suspended. The NFL is conducting its own investigation into an alleged incident of domestic violence by Jackson, who is not facing criminal prosecution because his case was assigned for diversion . Third-round pick Keagen Trost , who was expected to back up Jackson and Warren McClendon Jr ., left the preseason opener with a hamstring injury. Coach Sean McVay said he's hopeful Trost will return to start the season. -- Barshop 

 QB stat to know:  Stafford is coming off a career-high 46 passing touchdowns -- his third season with 40 or more passing scores. Those three seasons are tied for the most by any QB in NFL history along with Aaron Rodgers  and Tom Brady. However, Stafford has seen major regression following each season of 40 passing TDs -- including going from 41 to 20 in 2012 and going from 41 to 10 in 2022. -- ESPN Research 

 Best-case scenario for 2026, per FPI: 14-3 
 Worst-case scenario for 2026, per FPI: 9-8

 This season is a success if ...  the Rams win the Super Bowl. The Rams took steps to maximize the remaining time that Stafford wants to play, so expectations are sky-high for Los Angeles. -- Barshop 

 One key fantasy nugget: The Rams regularly isolate Adams in scoring position given his ability to win off the release. His 14 touchdown receptions on end zone throws last season were the second most in a season this century (Randy Moss had 16 in 2007). -- Bowen 

 Bold prediction for 2026: Tight end Terrance Ferguson will catch eight touchdown passes. I'm buying the hype here because it just makes too much sense. The Rams need a third pass catcher behind Nacua and Adams, and with a year of experience in the league after being a 2025 second-round pick, Ferguson could emerge as that guy. If either of those two receivers misses time, his ceiling could be even higher. -- Walder 

 
 Full schedule | Roster | Depth chart 
 Read more on the Rams 

 
 

 
 

 

 2. Buffalo Bills 
 Chances to make the playoffs: 84.1% 
 Chances to win division: 67.1% 
 Projected wins: 10.7 
 Strength of schedule: 14th easiest 
 2025 record: 12-5

 Biggest strength: Josh Allen . It's pretty simple. The Bills have an opportunity to win a Super Bowl once again this year, despite a first-time head coach, and that's because of who is playing quarterback. Allen, 30, is going into his ninth NFL season and has a new No. 1 receiver in DJ Moore . Breaking records has become commonplace for the 2024 MVP, and Allen gives the team a chance in every game. -- Alaina Getzenberg 

 Biggest concern: It is a transition year for the new defensive scheme. Coordinator Jim Leonhard has been open about the fact this year's defense will not fully look like his vision for the unit as it transitions from a 4-3 to 3-4 base. There is a mix of new players who fit the scheme specifically and carryovers from the previous regime. How the group comes together will go a long way in determining the unit's success. -- Getzenberg 

 QB stat to know:  Allen's dual-threat ability is unlike anything the NFL has seen. Allen already has 299 passing and rushing TDs combined in his first eight seasons, 40 more than the next-closest player ( Patrick Mahomes , 259). In fact, he already has the most through a player's first nine seasons (next closest: Peyton Manning, 288). -- ESPN Research 

 Best-case scenario for 2026, per FPI: 13-4 
 Worst-case scenario for 2026, per FPI: 8-9

 This season is a success if ...  the Bills reach the Super Bowl. Unfortunately for new coach Joe Brady, that's the bar. Maximizing Allen's tenure is the priority, and anything comparable to or less than what Sean McDermott accomplished won't make for a fully successful season. -- Getzenberg 

 One key fantasy nugget:  Allen gives fantasy managers a major boost when the Bills have the ball on the doorstep of the end zone. He converted 22 of 28 true goal-line carries (78.6%) over the past three seasons. -- Bowen 

 Bold prediction for 2026: Wide receiver Keon Coleman will record 750 or more receiving yards and at least five touchdowns -- both career highs. Earlier this offseason I thought there was a decent chance he'd be on a different team by now. But Coleman also hasn't been that bad in his first two years, posting a 49 overall score in ESPN's receiver score (just below average) and 1.6 yards per route run. Even though the Bills added Moore, I could see Coleman having a mini breakout in Year 3. -- Walder 

 
 Full schedule | Roster | Depth chart 
 Read more on the Bills 

 
 
 

 

 3. Seattle Seahawks 
 Chances to make the playoffs: 68.0% 
 Chances to win division: 26.3% 
 Projected wins: 10.2 
 Strength of schedule: Sixth hardest 
 2025 record: 14-3

 Biggest strength: The defense remains the strength even though it lost three players -- safety Coby Bryant , cornerback Riq Woolen and outside linebacker Boye Mafe - from the unit that allowed the fewest points in the NFL last season. The Seahawks still have plenty of difference-makers on that side of the ball, and they still have one of the game's brightest defensive minds, coach Mike Macdonald, calling the shots. -- Brady Henderson 

 Biggest concern: It's more of a question mark than a concern, but Sam Darnold and the offense will be relying on a first-time coordinator in Brian Fleury. Macdonald's choice to replace Klint Kubiak, Fleury will be running an offense that's similar to his predecessor's, but he will almost certainly have to endure some growing pains as he calls plays for the first time. -- Henderson 

 QB stat to know:  Darnold has won 14 games in each of the past two seasons, making him one of two quarterbacks in NFL history with consecutive 14-win seasons along with Tom Brady in 2003 and 2004. No quarterback has had three consecutive 14-win seasons. -- ESPN Research

title: 2026 NFL season sim: Predictions, surprises, playoff teams
summary: We played out one of the Football Power Index's 10,000 season simulations (No. 9,187), from Week 1 through Super Bowl LXI.
full_text:
Every preseason, we forecast possibilities for how the upcoming NFL season could pan out. Which teams  might emerge? Which teams  could go on a run? And which teams  should win the Super Bowl?

 But today is a day for absolutes. ESPN's  Football Power Index  simulates the season thousands of times to build our projections  ... but what if we look at only one simulation from the set? Just one possible outcome, one way things could play out. Life is a single simulation, after all.

 To be clear, what follows is neither my predictions nor the prognostications of ESPN Analytics. This is simply the story of simulation No. 9,187. Let's see how it plays out (with a little creative license woven in).

 See FPI's projections for the 2026 season 

 

 

 Hype on Bears and Texans falls very flat 
 These teams have been trendy preseason picks to go on deep playoff runs. But they didn't just miss the postseason in this simulation -- they weren't even close.

 

 For the Bears, it became apparent by midseason that the hoped-for growth in Year 2 under Ben Johnson wasn't going to happen. They were 3-6 through Week 10, with quarterback Caleb Williams still struggling with accuracy and the running game not enjoying the efficiency it showed in 2025.

 Houston's story was different. The Texans were 6-3 and firmly in the playoff race through 10 weeks, a game behind the Jaguars in the AFC South. But the version of C.J. Stroud we saw against the Patriots in the 2025 divisional playoffs  emerged in the second half of the season. And Houston's vaunted defense fell off dramatically, too. The result? An improbable eight-game losing streak to finish the season.

 Chicago and Houston sported 6-11 records, with both teams' fanbases focused on their top-10 picks in the 2027 NFL draft rather than the playoff runs they expected entering the season.

 
 

 Cowboys win a mediocre NFC East 
 With two weeks left, the Cowboys, Eagles and Giants were in a three-way tie with mediocre 7-8 records. It took weeks for Philadelphia to find its offensive rhythm under new coordinator  Sean Mannion. The Cowboys' new-look defense held up well early in the season but couldn't sustain that improvement, causing Dallas to enter the final two weeks on a four-game losing streak. The Giants' passing game struggled early with wide receiver Malik Nabers being limited but got better as he got healthier.

 All three teams had a shot at the playoffs with two games left. The Cowboys dealt a major blow to New York in Week 17, winning a 19-7 defensive battle. The Eagles upset the 49ers 23-19 on the road. But the Cowboys had the tiebreaker advantage, so Dallas took the division when it beat the Commanders in Week 18 even though Philadelphia prevailed over the Giants to finish with an identical 9-8 record.

 Dallas got the No. 4 seed in the NFC playoffs as the division winner with the worst record while the Eagles missed out. That earned the Cowboys a home wild-card game against the fifth-seeded, defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks. Dak Prescott lit up Seattle's defense, throwing two touchdowns to CeeDee Lamb in a 31-19 victory that had Cowboys fans dreaming of a trip to the Super Bowl.

 But it was not to be. The Cowboys lost 27-20 to the Lions in Detroit a week later to fall short of the conference championship round yet again.

 

 
 

 Chiefs retake the AFC West, Broncos miss the playoffs 
 The Chiefs won the AFC West nine seasons in a row from 2016 to 2024 and made three consecutive Super Bowls before a wildly disappointing 2025 campaign in which they finished 6-11 and missed the playoffs. Kansas City got back on top in 2026 -- of the division, at least.

 It was almost a wire-to-wire performance. The Chiefs took sole possession of first place after Week 4 and never gave it up despite the Chargers' best efforts. Patrick Mahomes rebounded to some degree, returning to being a top-five QBR passer but not the MVP. And receiver Rashee Rice finally achieved the full season of success that had previously eluded him.

 The 12-5 Chiefs earned the No. 2 seed in the AFC, with the Chargers making the playoffs as the No. 5 seed at 10-7. The Chargers got the last laugh, though, beating Kansas City 27-24 at Arrowhead Stadium in the divisional playoffs.

 As for the Broncos, who were arguably a Bo Nix injury short of making it to the Super Bowl a year ago? They regressed badly and finished 7-10.

 
 

 Patriots, Steelers fail to reach the postseason 
 The Patriots looked like they were going to back up their status as reigning AFC champions, sporting a 6-3 record and a 1½-game lead in the AFC East through Week 9. But New England stumbled against some heavy hitters, losing to the Lions, Chargers, Bills, Vikings and Broncos in the back half of the season. That resulted in a 9-8 record, which was not good enough for a wild-card spot, as the Pats lost tiebreakers to the Colts and Bengals.

 Pittsburgh also fell short in its first season under Mike McCarthy , missing the playoffs for the first time since 2022. Quarterback Aaron Rodgers was below average again, and the rest of the roster wasn't strong enough to make up for it, so the Steelers limped to an 8-9 record.

 

 
 

 Jaguars take the AFC South, but Colts steal their thunder 
 Jacksonville came out of the gates hot, with quarterback Trevor Lawrence picking up right where he left off in 2025. The Jaguars started the season 7-2 and pulled away after Houston imploded, clinching the division by Week 16. The Jaguars lost their final two games to finish 10-7 but safely made the playoffs as the No. 3 seed.

 Jacksonville earned the right to face division foe Indianapolis at home in the wild-card round. The Colts got into the playoffs by beating a Jaguars team that was resting its starters in Week 18 and repeated the feat against Jacksonville's A-team, shutting down Lawrence and the Jags' offense to win 18-12.

 It was a 180-degree reversal for Indianapolis, which lost its last seven games in 2025 to go from 8-2 to out of the playoffs. But the Colts' Cinderella run in 2026 ended with a 55-23 loss to top-seeded Buffalo in the divisional playoffs.

 
 

 Panthers start 0-7, but Jets earn the No. 1 draft pick 
 The Bryce Young era in Carolina ended at some point during the team's seven-game, season-opening losing streak. He's under contract for next year, but it became clear that Carolina was going to need to find another quarterback -- perhaps in the 2027 draft. But it won't be with the first pick. The Panthers played three different quarterbacks during the back half of the season and finished with a 6-4 burst to go 6-11, ending with the No. 4 pick.

 The honor of selecting first went to the Jets, who finished two games behind everyone else in going 2-15. So will the Jets draft  Arch Manning with the first pick? Dante Moore ? CJ Carr ? Darian Mensah ? Drew Mestemaker ? Trinidad Chambliss ? Someone else? New York is spoiled for choice, especially given its three first-round picks.

 
 

 Exceptional NFC West comes down to the wire ... 
 The NFC West boasts  three of FPI's top five teams entering 2026. Those preseason expectations came to fruition in simulation 9,187.

 Through 12 weeks, the Seahawks, 49ers and Rams were each 9-2 -- with only three of those six combined losses coming to teams outside the division! Fast forward to Week 18, with the 49ers and Seahawks entering their finales tied at 12-4 and the Rams one game back at 11-5. But the Rams came out firing in Week 18, blowing out the Seahawks 37-8. The 49ers destroyed the last-place Cardinals 30-3, securing not only the division but also the No. 1 seed in the NFC. Seattle and Los Angeles had to settle for the No. 5 and No. 6 seeds, respectively.

 So that had the 49ers feeling good entering the playoffs. Was this the year Kyle Shanahan and San Francisco would get over the Super Bowl hump?

 

 
 The Rams get the last laugh ... to an extent 
 All three NFC West stalwarts were considered Super Bowl contenders entering the…

title: Panthers banking on RBs Hubbard, Brooks despite injury histories
summary: Carolina wants to run the ball more, but how will each back -- including AJ Dillon -- handle the workload?
full_text:
Carolina Panthers coach Dave Canales wants to run the ball more, especially during the 2026 NFL season . He has made his intentions clear over the past three summers.

 And with offensive coordinator Brad Idzik now calling plays , and 2024 second-round pick Jonathon Brooks returning to the mix , Carolina is hoping for a boost in production and consistency from its running back rotation. After a couple of years of uneven production, the Panthers are counting on a trio of running backs with notable injury histories to get the ball moving: Brooks, Chuba Hubbard and AJ Dillon .

 Brooks, who was sidelined in practice last week because of general soreness, also missed Monday's workout. Canales said last Thursday that he was "very optimistic" about Brooks' availability in Week 1 against the Chicago Bears ( Sunday, 1 p.m. ET, Fox ). However, on Monday, Canales said he remained hopeful on Brooks but wouldn't give an update on his status until Wednesday.

 

 Brooks is expected to share the backfield workload in 2026 with Hubbard, the Panthers' returning starter, and as Rico Dowdle proved last season, having a tandem to ride the hot hand in the backfield is important in any offense.

 "Yeah, we'll definitely roll it out just the way we have been," Canales said last month. "Where you have a lead back for the series, the other guy comes in on third down so they can be in there for the protection, and also we run the ball on third down. So those are good opportunities to just keep a guy into the game, while the other person, whether it's Chuba or [Brooks], we'll make that decision when we get closer.

 "But whoever the lead guy for the base downs is, they'll get the bulk of that rhythm."

 Here's a breakdown of the Panthers' current running back depth chart and the latest news on their health:

 

 Chuba Hubbard | Age: 27 
 2025 stats: 511 rushing yards and a TD on 134 carries (3.8 yards per carry); 223 receiving yards and three TDs on 30 catches (7.4 yards per catch)

 Recent injury history: Hamstring injury (missed entire 2026 preseason); calf injury (missed two games in 2025)

 Hubbard was hampered by the aforementioned calf injury throughout the 2025 season, despite missing only two games. He eventually lost his starting job to Dowdle -- who is now in Pittsburgh -- and finished with a forgettable stat total in the Panthers' push toward a playoff spot. After winning the NFC South title, Hubbard once again became the primary back in the team's wild-card loss to the Los Angeles Rams .

 Hubbard appeared to be on a load management schedule throughout training camp. While he frequently worked with the starting group in practice, the first-team reps were spread out. The veteran playmaker sustained a hamstring injury midway through camp, and he missed the entirety of the preseason game slate. He also missed out on joint practices with the Jacksonville Jaguars and Houston Texans .

 Hubbard returned to practice last week. Prior to the preseason finale, he said he could have played in the final game if it had been a meaningful matchup. But the Panthers rested their starters and took precautions with Hubbard throughout the summer. Resting Hubbard for a big workload appears to be the plan.

 Hubbard, who signed a four-year, $33.2 million contract extension in 2024, has been backed by Canales and general manager Dan Morgan at every turn, and their hope is he can return to the form that warranted his long-term pact in the first place. He ran for 1,195 yards and 10 touchdowns in 2024 before his injury-plagued 2025 campaign.

 

 Jonathon Brooks | Age: 23 
 2025 stats: N/A

 Recent injury history: Tore right ACL in 2023 (at Texas) and in 2024 (he missed entire 2025 season and only played in three games in 2024)

 Brooks made his training camp and preseason debuts this summer. During the previous two offseasons, Brooks was sidelined as he recovered from ACL surgeries on his right knee. The No. 46 overall pick in the 2024 draft initially injured his knee while playing for the Longhorns. But during his rookie season, Brooks returned to the field in Week 12 and played in three games before retearing his right ACL against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 14.

 

 After missing the entire 2025 season, he returned to practices in the spring and has had a steady workload ever since. The Panthers have been patient with Brooks in his recovery, and he had the occasional rest day sprinkled into the workout schedule.

 The Panthers are hoping he can become a home run threat in the offense. He displayed excellent hands as a receiver out of the backfield in training camp. And while his preseason rushing stats (23 yards and a touchdown on eight carries) and pass protection won't wow anyone, Brooks has looked confident while rushing into contact.

 Brooks, if available for Week 1, is likely to be used as a change-of-pace partner for Hubbard -- who is more of a traditional north-south runner -- throughout drives.

 The Panthers aren't likely to have an even workload split right away, but Hubbard and Brooks will share reps in the backfield immediately, depending on the latter's health. If Brooks can make big plays early and prove his durability in the first month of the season, he could become the top back in the rotation soon enough.

 

 AJ Dillon | Age: 28 
 2025 stats: 60 rushing yards on 12 carries (5.0 yards per carry); three catches for 21 yards (7 yards per catch)

 Recent injury history: Neck stingers in 2023 and 2024 (he missed entire 2024 season)

 Dillon entered camp as a long shot after a forgettable one-year stint with the Eagles in 2025. Dillon -- who missed the entire 2024 season with the Green Bay Packers with a neck injury -- played in seven games for the Eagles, and he was a healthy scratch for the other 10 games.

 However, during the Panthers' preseason, Dillon proved his worth as a receiver, runner and special teams asset. Dillon ran 14 times for 46 yards and two touchdowns and caught eight passes for 75 yards. He also played 10 snaps on special teams, as he was used as a wing blocker on the punt team.

 Dillon could be used occasionally on third down as a short-yardage back, especially with the Panthers opposing QB sneaks with quarterback Bryce Young . He could also be used on third down as a blocker and receiver out of the backfield. That said, it's worth noting that Canales, historically, has rarely used his third back on offense when his top two options have been healthy and available.

 
 Practice squad options: Anthony Tyus III , Ahmani Marshall 
 Tyus spent all of last season on the practice squad before returning to Carolina for the offseason program and training camp. He produced 127 rushing yards and a lost fumble on a team-leading 31 carries in the preseason; he also caught all five of his targets for 24 yards and a touchdown.

 Marshall was added to the roster last week. He previously played for the Cleveland Browns , who waived him during the cut-down deadline last month. Marshall appeared in all three preseason games for Cleveland, producing 46 rushing yards, 48 receiving yards and a touchdown catch on 29 total touches. A 2025 undrafted free agent out of Appalachian State, the Winston-Salem native has yet to appear in a regular-season game.

title: NFL execs predict 2026 award winners: MVP, top rookies, more
summary: Who will win MVP? Who will take Offensive and Defensive Rookie of the Year? Who is primed for a breakout? We asked execs and scouts for their picks.
full_text:
The march to the ultimate stage -- Super Bowl LXI on Feb. 14, in SoFi Stadium -- begins Wednesday, when the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks square off at Lumen Field (8:20 p.m. ET, NBC). The Los Angeles Rams are the trendy Super Bowl pick in league circles. But keep in mind this is the era of ultimate parity. At this time last year, the Seahawks and Patriots had 60-1 and 80-1 odds to win the Super Bowl, respectively.

 The journey to a championship will unfold alongside brilliant individual efforts. The hunt for league MVP will be defined by elite quarterback play. Other top awards at the annual NFL Honors will highlight the game's best.

 We asked league executives and scouts to sort out who will hold the hardware when the 2026 season ends. From MVP to rookies and coach of the year, few of the major awards offer a clear consensus at this early stage. The possibilities are endless and enticing.

 
 Jump to: 
 MVP  | OPOY  | DPOY  | OROY  | DROY 
 Comebacks  |  Breakouts  |  Top coach 

 
 

 

 

 MVP: Joe Burrow , Cincinnati Bengals 
 None of the top quarterbacks in their primes are controversial picks. The top four passers between ages 29 and 30 -- Patrick Mahomes , Josh Allen , Lamar Jackson and Joe Burrow -- have been selected in this very exercise as MVP predictions from 2021 through 25. Only Burrow lacks the actual hardware. But he slightly edges the field here, despite a push from Los Angeles' Justin Herbert and reservations about Burrow's durability.

 In his last full season (2024) he threw for 4,918 yards and 43 touchdowns. Health is the primary issue holding him back. "He senses the urgency this year and is talking like it -- I think he's ready to back it up," an AFC executive said. "If he stays healthy. Big if."

 

 The Bengals' offense will evolve this year, featuring more under-center work, which could open up a running game that ranked 29th last year.

 Allen, meanwhile, is looking to join Aaron Rodgers , Jackson and Mahomes as active players with multiple MVPs.

 "I'm done banking on Burrow because of the injuries," an AFC exec said. "I would, if not for health issues. Stafford won't get it again, Mahomes is coming back from injury, and even though you can't count out Lamar, he's taken a step back. Allen is the safest bet."

 As for Herbert, people inside the league value his work much more highly than some factions of the internet do. "Don't think he got enough credit for everything he did last year when the OL got decimated by injuries," an NFC exec said. "They get healthy and a proven, creative playcaller that can make his life easier and [offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel] hasn't had a QB this gifted."

 Also receiving votes:   Justin Herbert ( Los Angeles Chargers ), Josh Allen ( Buffalo Bills )

 

 
 

 Offensive Player of the Year: Jahmyr Gibbs , Detroit Lions 
 Running backs have won three of the past six OPOY awards, and Gibbs might be next. He has made back-to-back-to-back Pro Bowls despite averaging 225 carries per year as a 1A option alongside David Montgomery . He still managed 39 rushing touchdowns, or one every 17th rushing attempt. And he caught 77 passes for 616 yards last season.

 "He'll rise to the occasion as the lead back, the Lions will be competitive and they'll probably be in a lot of shootouts, which will help Gibbs' production," a veteran NFL scout said.

 It's worth noting Detroit entered the week with minimal experience behind Gibbs. Backups Sione Vaki and Jacob Saylors have combined for nine NFL rushing attempts. Veteran Isiah Pacheco is on injured reserve.

 Neither Gibbs nor Atlanta's Bijan Robinson has won this award despite the duo jockeying for tailback supremacy. That could change this year.

 Also receiving votes:   Ja'Marr Chase ( Cincinnati Bengals ), Bijan Robinson ( Atlanta Falcons )

 

 
 

 Defensive Player of the Year: Will Anderson Jr ., Houston Texans 
 Anderson can become the fifth edge rusher in the past six years to win this award. Fending off reigning champ Myles Garrett won't be easy, but voters in such exercises often like to predict ascending young players breaking the mold.

 

 Anderson is 25, squarely in his prime and has improved his sack total in each of his first three seasons, from seven to 11 to 12. Houston has a realistic chance to represent the AFC in the Super Bowl thanks to a vaunted defense led by Anderson.

 "He can have the type of 15-sack season that will define him, especially with Danielle Hunter on the other side," an NFL personnel evaluator said. "You can't double both. He can be the leader of that defense, which is just nasty."

 Also receiving votes:   Myles Garrett ( Los Angeles Rams )

 

 
 

 Offensive Rookie of the Year: Jadarian Price , Seattle Seahawks 
 This was a close race among the top two running backs selected in the 2026 draft (both out of Notre Dame), an ascending player out of Cleveland and a QB2 in the AFC West.

 Price, the 32nd overall pick by the reigning champion Seahawks, has impressed head coach Mike Macdonald with his coachability and open-field vision. In fact, some in Seattle feel Price can add a new dimension to the running game, despite new Kansas City Chief Kenneth Walker III's consistent production over four years.

 Price is playing for an elite team as a potential lead option. Seattle plans to use two or three backs as part of each game plan, but Price should be showcased a lot.

 "He's the best they've got, and that offense is dedicated to running the ball," an NFC scout said. "Zach Charbonnet isn't ready yet."

 Also receiving votes: Jeremiyah Love ( Arizona Cardinals ), KC Concepcion ( Cleveland Browns ), Fernando Mendoza ( Las Vegas Raiders )

 

 
 

 Defensive Rookie of the Year: Caleb Downs , Dallas Cowboys 
 The Cowboys have big plans for Downs, who instantly becomes one of Dallas' most versatile players.

 When I asked head coach Brian Schottenheimer at training camp where Downs is best served on the field, he said "anywhere," then pointed out that he can cover star receiver CeeDee Lamb up the seam.

 The Cowboys will play Downs primarily in the slot, where he can disrupt in the open field. "He will play in the middle of the defense so he will probably have some ball production and high tackle numbers," an AFC executive said. "And if he helps turn around Dallas' defense, he'll be looked at as a catalyst."

 

 The last defensive back to win DROY was Sauce Gardner in 2022, when he recorded two interceptions and 20 pass deflections. Ball production is a must in order to win this award.

 Also receiving votes: Rueben Bain Jr. ( Tampa Bay Buccaneers ), Mansoor Delane ( Kansas City Chiefs ), R Mason Thomas (Chiefs), David Bailey ( New York Jets )

 

 
 

 Comeback Player of the Year: Patrick Mahomes , Kansas City Chiefs 
 This one is set up for Mahomes like a well-blocked bubble screen. The three-time Super Bowl MVP has crushed his rehab from a torn ACL and PCL. He's poised to play in Week 1. The offense should be better overall, with a Walker-led running game and a healthier receiving corps.

 And, perhaps for the first time in his career, a hint of doubt hovers over Mahomes and his place in the quarterback pantheon. He has had multiple down years (by his standards) statistically. "He's such an elite competitor and player that I'm counting on him responding," an AFC scout said. "He hears the noise."

 Also receiving votes: Kyler Murray ( Minnesota Vikings ), Aaron Donald ( Los Angeles Rams ), Jayden Daniels ( Washington Commanders )

 

 
 

 Breakout player: Matthew Golden , Green Bay Packers 
 Last year was a roller coaster for Golden, who earned rave reviews in 2025 training camp, then spent the season as a tertiary option. He finished the season with 29 catches for 361 yards on 44 targets. All of those totals ranked outside of the top three among Packers weapons last year.

 

 The departure of Romeo Doubs opens a spot for Golden in the team's three-receiver sets alongside Christian Watson and Jayden…

title: Todd Monken, QBs, the Browns and a lifetime in pursuit
summary: At age 60, the first-time head coach brings to Cleveland a gritty resolve, an ability to cut through to QBs and a dream that this will be "my last job."
full_text:
TODD MONKEN'S ENTRY into the coaching ranks seemed predestined, but the same couldn't be said for an ascension to one of the top jobs in the NFL.

 However, after three-plus decades of chasing a dream, a monthlong hiring process and three rounds of days-long interviews, Monken finally got the news of a lifetime from the Cleveland Browns .

 In late January, Browns owner Jimmy Haslam texted Monken to ask if he could join yet another video call meeting. At this point, Monken knew the hiring process was nearing its end, so he asked if he could wear a sweatshirt instead of a suit.

 Haslam obliged, and when the two connected, the owner asked if Monken was wearing Browns paraphernalia.

 

 "I said, 'No, but I can take a crayon here and draw a logo on it like a fifth-grader,'" Monken recalled to NFL Network at the scouting combine in February. "... Even throughout the whole process, I've had other opportunities and to not get one of those jobs, [it's] not that you come to the thought that you'll never get one, but to finally have it come to fruition, again, pretty neat."

 Monken turned 60 on Feb. 5, two days after the Browns introduced him as the franchise's 19th noninterim head coach and 11th since returning to Cleveland in 1999. He had enjoyed a decades-long career in coaching, and had this Browns opening not worked out, he had a job waiting for him as the New York Giants ' offensive coordinator, working with former boss John Harbaugh.

 Now, in what outsiders are already calling a lost season primed to take advantage of a hyped 2027 quarterback draft class, Monken has set his sights on maximizing the QBs he has on the roster and a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity as a first-time NFL head coach, beginning Sunday on the road against the Jacksonville Jaguars ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ). People who know Monken best say his passion, intellect and ability to connect with others can cut through for a young Cleveland team in need of a firm culture and new identity after winning just eight games over the past two seasons.

 "I'm not getting any younger, let's be real honest here," Monken said at his introductory news conference. "Although I'll say this, the version you're getting of me now is a hell of a lot better than it would have been 15, 20 years ago."

 
 

 
 COINCIDENTALLY, CLEVELAND'S PRESEASON opener against the Chicago Bears on Aug. 15 brought Monken back to the roots of his almost-40-year rise through the coaching ranks.

 In Wheaton, a suburb about 30 miles west of Chicago, Monken grew up in a football family with a storied history. His father, Bob, was a legendary coach at Lake Park High School in Roselle, Illinois, for 30 years. As the Browns' plane descended into Chicago, Monken could spot the football fields that were named after his father.

 "Todd's from a kind of coaching royalty in Illinois," said Randy Oberembt, Monken's football coach at Knox College (Illinois).

 Monken's dad, along with four uncles who all coached high school football in the area, was inducted into the Illinois Coaches Hall of Fame. The five Monken boys had seven sons, all of whom got into coaching at some level. Monken's coaching generation also includes his cousin Jeff, who is the head football coach at Army. Monken's 25-year-old son, Travis, is an offensive analyst with the Browns.

 "I think as kids, we loved the game because we saw our dads loved the game and put that joy into football," Jeff Monken told ESPN. "There were a lot of us that followed our fathers into that profession. Not every single Monken boy cousin did it, but darn near all of us."

 At its essence, though, Monken's father and his mother, Jo Ellen, a second-grade teacher, were educators. That upbringing served as the foundation for everything Monken has done as a football coach. Joe Ellen died in 2023 and Bob died in 2024.

 "We didn't make a ton of money. We didn't have that," Monken told ESPN. "But what they did for me, helping me, engaged in our lives and then disciplining me, I think that's where you see highly successful people; that is the starting point. That's not the end-all. There's plenty of people that were as lucky as I am, but I'm just saying that gives you a f---ing head start. To me, that's where privilege comes from."

 

 
 DESTINED TO FOLLOW in his forebears' footsteps, Monken began his college career as a quarterback at Western Illinois -- "I realized I could evaluate talent and I wasn't very good" -- but then transferred to the College of DuPage, a junior college, where he played baseball before landing at Division III Knox College.

 "I knew then at that moment I wanted to coach," Monken told ESPN. "I helped my dad out my first year at the junior college, and I knew I wanted to coach. I loved it, loved being part of a team. So I thought if I wanted to coach, I felt like I had to play. I felt like I had to go play, whether I was right or wrong."

 Years before he inherited Cleveland's quarterback quandary and oversaw the competition between Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders , Monken was in the middle of his own at Knox. He was in a quarterback competition with the incumbent, multiyear starter and All-American Bob Monroe. After suffering an injury and spending his first season at Knox as a backup, Monken split playing time with Monroe in his second season; Monroe played the first and third quarters, while Monken played the second and fourth quarters.

 As odd as the dynamic was, it failed to cause friction between the two then and now; they have remained close friends after their playing days. Monroe was even in attendance for Monken's introduction as the Browns' head coach.

 

 The next season, with Monroe graduating, Monken became a full-time starter and was named a 1988 Division III All-American, leading the nation in pass attempts, completions and completion percentage. He was also a two-sport athlete, lettering in baseball, and was inducted into the athletic department's hall of fame.

 "We wanted him to stay with us for another year, and we would've gladly turned the offense over to him in 1989, but he wanted to get into [coaching]," Oberembt told ESPN.

 "And that to me was very telling because he was willing to go up to Grand Valley State, be a [graduate assistant] without really knowing what was going to happen up there. And it turned out that that was one of the great coaching laboratories in college football, if you look at what those guys went on and did. And then the rest of his trips, I think what we learned is he was always willing to take the hard job, and he's a ferocious worker."

 
 MONKEN BEGAN HIS coaching journey at Grand Valley State as a graduate assistant in 1989 -- he worked alongside then-defensive coordinator Brian Kelly -- and then bounced around the country in various assistant roles. This also included a four-year stint from 2007 to 2010 in Jacksonville as the Jaguars' wide receivers coach.

 At his higher-profile stops, a theme in Monken's coaching résumé emerged: He could connect with all types of quarterbacks and produce high-octane offenses. There was Brandon Weeden at Oklahoma State. Monken's lone head-coaching job was at Southern Mississippi, where he inherited a winless program and brought it a conference championship with Nick Mullens by Year 3.

 "The difference with him was he has an extremely high level of confidence," former Oklahoma State coach Mike Gundy told ESPN. "I would go in his office and ask him what he thought about the game this week. And he would say, 'I'll be disappointed if we have to punt one time.' And he was serious. ... And he always had the ability to instill a high level of confidence in the players."

 Similar success for Monken carried into the NFL, when Dirk Koetter tapped him to be the Buccaneers' offensive coordinator. But after a forgettable one-year stint in Cleveland in 2019 -- Monken was the OC for Freddie Kitchens but didn't call plays during a disappointing 6-10 season -- the staff was fired, and Monken…

title: NFC East: Sizing up the Cowboys, Eagles, Giants and Commanders
summary: Our reporters discuss what needs to go right for the Eagles, Cowboys, Commanders and Giants in 2026.
full_text:
Week 1 of the 2026 season kicks off with the NFC East rival  New York Giants , Dallas Cowboys , Philadelphia Eagles and Washington Commanders  playing against each other Sunday -- Commanders at Eagles ( 4:25 p.m. ET, Fox ), Cowboys at Giants ( 8:20 p.m. ET, NBC ) --  so there's added importance on getting off to a good start.

 For the Cowboys and Commanders, it's even more imperative since they meet in Week 2 at AT&T Stadium.

 Last season, the Eagles became the first team to repeat as division champion since the 2003 and 2004 seasons, and Philadelphia looks to become the first to three-peat since coach Andy Reid's Eagles owned the division from 2001 to 2004.

 There has been plenty of change in the division with John Harbaugh becoming the head coach of the Giants and every team but the Cowboys employing a new offensive coordinator. The Eagles are the only team not welcoming a new defensive coordinator.

 Eagles reporter Tim McManus, Cowboys reporter Todd Archer, Giants reporter Jordan Raanan and Commanders reporter John Keim take a look at some key topics in the NFC East, where the Eagles are the odds-on favorites (+122) over the Cowboys (+184), Commanders (+600) and Giants (+600), according to DraftKings Sportsbook.

 

 

 Expectation for quarterbacks 

 Eagles 

 Jalen Hurts has a new offensive coordinator -- again -- and this time is adapting to an overhauled scheme installed by up-and-comer Sean Mannion that will ask him to lean into elements of the game that he hasn't majored in before, such as being under center and throwing over the middle of the field. The Eagles knew they needed a reboot after the highest-salaried offense in the NFL finished 23 rd in passing yards (194.3), 19 th in Total QBR (52.9) and points per game (22.3) and first in three-and-outs last season.

 The passing game was largely boom or bust this summer, as Hurts found receivers in rhythm and made some pretty throws deep down the field but also tossed double-digit interceptions, more than we're accustomed to seeing out of him. Hurts' career has been defined 1) by winning and 2) by rising to the challenge. Count this among his toughest tests, as he takes the reins of a new system to begin the post A.J. Brown era.  -- Tim McManus 

 

 Cowboys 

 It feels safe to pencil in  Dak Prescott  for a 4,500-yard, 30-touchdown season since he has essentially done that in his last four full seasons. He's now 33 and in his 11th season, so he knows what defenses are doing to try to impact him and feels as if he has the answers to the test before given the exam. He showed up to training camp wearing a Super Bowl XXX throwback T-shirt, hoping to manifest Super Bowl feelings for this year's team. Something to consider: He has not missed the playoffs in consecutive years when he has started more than half of the Cowboys' games.  -- Todd Archer 

   Giants 

 Jaxson Dart should take the next step in Year 2. He did some nice things as a rookie, rushing for nine scores while throwing 15 touchdown passes to five interceptions. But now he needs to take his game to the next level in a new offense coordinated by Matt Nagy. If he does, the Giants' season will be a success. If he doesn't, it will be disappointing. For Dart to get to the next level, he will have to get the ball out quicker and make more anticipatory throws within the offense. Just flashes of brilliance won't be enough. Dart has to show he's a quarterback that you can not only win with, but win a Super Bowl with as the starter.  -- Jordan Raanan 

 Commanders 

 Very high. Daniels has always been an accurate passer, but he looked even sharper throughout training camp. Offensive coordinator David Blough said he's as "accurate as he's ever been." But his quick command of a new offense -- how he handles the huddle, what he's telling teammates as they break it or walk to the line -- has also been impressive. He remains a dynamic playmaker, capable of turning bad plays into explosive ones. Washington has surrounded him with his strongest cast of passing targets -- having added tight end Chig Okonkwo and receivers Stefon Diggs and rookie Antonio Williams to pair with Terry McLaurin  -- in his three seasons with the team.  -- John Keim 

 

 

 How each team win the division 

 Eagles 

 It will be on the strength of the defense and the ground game. The key to Philly's success over the years has been in the trenches. The offensive line took a step back last season but enters this year generally healthy. That's good news for Saquon Barkley , who showed in 2024 that he can be downright dominant when working in tandem with a sound front.

 The defense is in Year 3 under Vic Fangio and has a chance to be a top-three unit in the NFL. Defensive tackle Jalen Carter looks healthy and ready to wreck games, and the secondary boasts arguably the best cornerback trio in the league in Quinyon Mitchell , Cooper DeJean and Riq Woolen . This group is capable of carrying the team early as the offense finds its way.  -- McManus 

 

 Cowboys 

 If Prescott stays healthy, the Cowboys will have a shot. He is 37-10 all-time against the Eagles, Giants and Commanders. The Cowboys' offense figures to be strong; maybe stronger than it was last season. A second year with coach Brian Schottenheimer calling the plays with Prescott, wide receiver  CeeDee Lamb , wide receiver George Pickens , running back Javonte Williams and tight end Jake Ferguson  makes the offense formidable, but can the defense do enough? There were promising signs in the preseason, and if defensive coordinator Christian Parker can get all of the new faces playing together quickly, the Cowboys can break the Eagles' two-year hold on the division.  -- Archer 

   Giants 

 It will take a lot. A ton needs to go right for the Giants, who have won only seven games in the past two years combined. First, they will need to win the opener at home Sunday night against the Cowboys. New York can't be losing to division rivals in its home opener, especially with the loaded  Los Angeles Rams  on deck on a Monday night in Week 2. The Giants will have to be one of the best running teams in the league and have their defense make massive leaps, especially a secondary that has questions at every position.  -- Raanan

This also assumes the Eagles take a step back -- at some point this will happen, right? -- and Dallas' defense still can't help its elite offense. Washington's main offseason focus was improving arguably the NFL's worst defense in 2025, adding high-profile pass rusher Odafe Oweh and drafting linebacker Sonny Styles among other moves. The Commanders are longer and faster in the front seven. Also, Daniels is coming off his best camp of his three seasons. It's not far-fetched to see him topping his rookie year. title: C.J. Stroud confident ahead of the biggest season of his life
summary: After a rocky end in the playoffs last season, it appears Stroud will play Year 4 without a new contract.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- Quarterback C.J. Stroud sported a large white T-shirt and baggy gray shorts as he drove to Reliant Stadium around 7 a.m. on July 28. He casually strolled into the  Houston Texans ' facility, reporting for his fourth training camp while the team's social media crew recorded his arrival.

 Minutes later, they posted the video on X, and the clip spread like a contagion across social media -- generating over 20 million views and sparking feedback about Stroud's "back-to-school" look.

 Stroud, who has family and close friends run his accounts, tries to avoid scrolling on social media, but even a post from "Maxisnicee," who reenacted Stroud's training camp entrance, got a reaction out of Stroud -- who posted laughing emojis under the Instagram video.

 "Max, that's my boy. I was tired," Stroud told ESPN with a laugh. "I was focused on doing my job and getting better that day, not what I was wearing. Sometimes you can't in life be super hard on yourself. ... I laugh at a lot of stuff because it's funny."

 

 Although the entrance to the building inspired jokes, the fact remains that Stroud is entering a pivotal Year 4. He hopes to play well enough to wash away the memories of last year's playoff struggles. According to DeMeco Ryans, the offseason and training camp were an excellent start -- with the Texans' coach saying Stroud "handled himself tremendously."

 "He's done a really good job of commanding the offense," Ryans said. "Great job of communicating with everyone, offensive line, receivers, tight ends, running backs. He's done a great job just having all those guys together, leading, speaking up in meetings, doing all those things you expect from your starting quarterback."

 That's Step 1 for Stroud, whose contract situation has been a talking point this offseason, but ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported Wednesday that "the current sentiment is Stroud will most likely not end up with a new deal" before Sunday's season opener.

 All of that should become clear this week after a deadline was set.

 "If we don't get it figured out before the season starts, then it'll be something we address in the offseason," general manager Nick Caserio said.

 The season starts against the Buffalo Bills , and according to league sources, both sides are content with Stroud's lack of a contract extension. It gives the Texans an extra year of evaluation and allows Stroud to bet on himself.

 Houston picked up Stroud's fifth-year option of his rookie deal in April, so he's still under contract in 2027. If he can get back to the trajectory he showed as a rookie, he could eventually sign a record-setting deal.

 Houston has shown that it will invest in its players, resetting the market with cornerback Derek Stingley Jr . (2025), and Will Anderson Jr . this offseason, which made him the highest-paid non-QB in NFL history .

 It's not a secret, however, that if Stroud struggles, questions about his future in Houston will continue.

 "Pressure is a privilege," Stroud said. "I'm excited. I've always been challenged in my career. I've always had to persevere through things, and I think this is something that I'm grateful for. I didn't wake up and forget how to play football."

 

 

 A DOWNPOUR OF scrutiny has rained down on Stroud since the Texans' season-ending loss to the New England Patriots in the divisional round of the playoffs.

 His four-interception performance (all in the first half) birthed offseason chatter ranging from whether Houston should trade him or pay him .

 Criticism isn't rare to Stroud, having learned to deal with it since his days at Ohio State. He has developed ways to ignore the noise, but something as simple as picking up his phone can open a gateway to negativity because of things such as social media.

 

 "People are quick to use Twitter," Stroud said. "I focus on me. I can't control [social media], so why would I care? Of course I'm human. I learned if some people had the opportunity to be me, they would. But a lot of people have opinions and don't have opportunities.

 "So the more opinions people have, the more opportunity that I have to prove who I am. They love to critique. That's part of life. I play in an entertainment sport, so they're critical of a lot of people. I have the opportunity to go play. No one can stop that."

 It will take a strong season to remove the stench from his last playoff game. But he feels he has been able to navigate the aftermath -- in part because it reminded him that failure doesn't define him.

 "I'm proud of myself for how I've handled these past couple months," Stroud said. "Yeah, I have things that I want back and mistakes that I made. But truly, God has worked through my shortcomings. If I was perfect, I wouldn't be able to be coachable or have the fear of God. So I'm glad that I have made mistakes."

 Through the scrutiny, Stroud's teammates have galvanized around their quarterback, as they know they'll need him at his best for a potential Super Bowl run.

 "He's built for everything," wide receiver Nico Collins told ESPN. "We believe in him, we love him. This is the best position he can be in right now. I feel like he is about to go out and show the whole world what he's made of, and I can't wait. We got his back 100%, all the way."

 

 
 SINCE A HISTORIC rookie season, Stroud's play has careened between flashes of brilliance and stretches of frustration. It has led to this crossroads of what to pay Stroud, and when to pay him. Stroud, though, has left negotiations to his agent, David Mulugheta, and has zeroed in on football.

 "You have to keep the main thing the main thing," Stroud said the day after his viral video was posted. "You have to just focus on one day at a time, one play and the football is what's gotten me to even have the conversation, to be able to get a second contract. I have to focus on football."

 

 Stroud ended 2023 as the Offensive Rookie of the Year, and he earned a Pro Bowl selection after throwing for 4,108 yards (the third most by a rookie in NFL history) and 23 touchdowns against just five interceptions.

 The yards and touchdowns were career highs. The interceptions were a career low. Yet it almost feels ancient.

 In 2024, he had 3,727 passing yards with 20 touchdowns and 12 interceptions. In 2025, he finished with 3,041 passing yards, 19 touchdowns and eight interceptions.

 Things weren't all negative though, as ESPN Analytics had him with the fifth-lowest turnover rate, 11th-best QBR and eighth-best expected points added per dropback (.19) last season. He also hasn't missed the playoffs since entering the league, and each year, the Texans have won their playoff opener.

 But going into 2026, Houston feels like it's a Super Bowl contender -- despite never advancing past the divisional round -- behind one of the league's best defenses.

 "Every year we always go short of that third round," Collins said. "I feel like this year, it's time to take that leap and go where we need to go."

 

 THE TEXANS BELIEVE the playcalling should be improved in Year 2 under offensive coordinator Nick Caley, with Houston ranking 18th in total offense (327 yards) and 16th in offensive points per game (21.9) last season.

 During training camp, Caley said, "I want to give ourselves an opportunity to play our best football when it matters the most." It's a reference to the playoffs where he and his quarterback must rise to the occasion.

 The synergy between quarterback and playcaller is vital. In June, Caley said he and Stroud have been able to "dive deeper" into their working relationship, and throughout camp he felt Stroud's process was stellar and that he was "even-keeled every day."

 "The ability to move on from a good play to the next play, a bad play to the next play, Stroud's demeanor has been awesome," Caley said. "His approach, his process, it's been consistent. It's really been consistent since spring, and I'm proud of him."

 Caserio echoed that sentiment in the spring.

title: Life after football: Joshua Kelley's path to filmmaking after the NFL
summary: We caught up with former Chargers player Joshua Kelley about life and filmaking after his NFL career.
full_text:
SINCE JOSHUA KELLEY  was 8 years old, his life was almost all about football.

 He finally started living out his dream of playing in the NFL when the Los Angeles Chargers selected him in the fourth round of the 2020 draft out of UCLA. Through four seasons with the Chargers, Kelley was a rotational running back and special teams contributor, totaling 1,148 yards and six touchdowns.

 When his rookie contract expired, Kelley joined the New York Giants for training camp then the Tennessee Titans for the 2024 season. As the season went on, however, he began to realize his priorities had changed. On team plane rides his mind was elsewhere, often in some alternate universe he'd created in his notebook. He began to dread team meetings, wanting to instead stay in his hotel room and write out the scenes of movies that cycled through his head.

 

 "That's when I kind of knew it was kind of done for me," Kelley told ESPN. "When that Sunday morning, that jittery, feeling kind of was not there anymore."

 Kelley hasn't officially retired from the NFL yet -- he jokes that he is keeping the door open just in case -- but as the 2026 campaign is set to kick off, he is transitioning into a new season of his own, as a filmmaker. Kelley, 28, wrote, directed and self-financed two short films this summer, one of which stars his former Chargers teammate  Keelan Doss . Kelley's first film, " No Chaser , " premiered Aug. 29 on YouTube.

 As Kelley's playing career reached its conclusion, he had something of an identity crisis, but through filmmaking he has found a new purpose, and he hopes to give that to other former players.

 "For us as football players, just athletes in general, once we're done playing, it's scary," Kelley said. "I just wanted to show athletes that it's possible to pivot and do your thing."

 

 A LARGE PART of Kelley's childhood was spent at the movie theater with his brother, Daniel, watching Spider-Man or other superhero films. When he wasn't at the theater, he was watching animated shows including "Naruto," "Dragon Ball Z" and "One Piece" and playing video games such as Final Fantasy, Kingdom Hearts and The Legend of Zelda.

 Kelley describes his hometown of Lancaster, California, as "the middle of nowhere," but these alternate realities allowed him to be anywhere he wanted to be.

 "It just kind of worked my brain," he said. "It's like a muscle that I developed over time, and then that love for it just came out to creative writing."

 But those creative muscles always took a back seat to football -- until Kelley didn't have football anymore.

 

 After the 2023 NFL season, Kelley was excited about what was next. His rookie contract was ending, meaning he was entering free agency for the first time, and he had an opportunity to potentially choose where he'd land.

 But Kelley went seven months without suiting up for an NFL team. At his home in Los Angeles, he felt a mix of embarrassment and confusion about his identity.

 "It gets real. All of a sudden, the people that are blowing up your line every day to congratulate you after the game, they're not doing that anymore," he said.

 "I was going through something, and I was like, 'Dang, who am I?'"

 While he was waiting for a call from an NFL team, Kelley's screenwriting journey began in earnest. His life was different without having to be at mandatory team offseason programming, allowing him to spend more time with his wife, Mikaela, and his son, Elijah. (The Kelleys now have another son, Caleb, who was born in April.) Still, Kelley set aside a few hours each day to write.

 "He would always be like, 'Look, I need to go in the room, be by myself and write,'" Mikaela said. "'During that time, I'd be like, 'Dude, what are you even working on?'"

 

 Kelley was excited to return to the NFL in October 2024 when he signed with the Titans, and he remained in Tennessee throughout the rest of the season. He didn't see much playing time, appearing in just three games and getting one carry for 2 yards, but his writing journey continued in the background.

 It was with Tennessee, on the team planes, in hotels and even in the locker room, where Kelley wrote an entire series about a football player going through a mental health crisis. Kelley wrote about 4,000 pages over the course of that year using his and friends' experiences to create the comedy-drama.

 That exploratory script ended up getting Kelley his first taste of Hollywood.

 After Kelley's agent, Bill Douglas at the entertainment and sports agency Paradigm, saw the script, he forwarded it to Dan Fogelman, Jess Rosenthal and Kevin Falls, the executive producers of an upcoming Hulu TV series, "The Land." The show is focused on a family involved in the Cleveland Browns organization, and they were looking for writers with professional football experience.

 "We really liked his scenes that were off the football field," Falls told ESPN. "You really get the feeling of a young couple and everyone thinks, 'Oh, that's a glamorous life.' And many times it is, but you get to see all of it."

 Kelley joined "The Land" as an entry-level staff writer in February 2025, shortly after the Titans' season ended. For the next five months, he helped shape key elements of the show. One character, Zeke, is modeled after Kelley's life. Kelley crafted most of Zeke's story, which includes the tension that comes with life outside of football: navigating media, marriage and personal life.

 "Most writers at the lower levels get rewritten extensively, sometimes higher levels too, but Joshua contributed," Falls said. "Joshua will have the pride of ownership when he sees his episode and know, 'Hey, that's me. I wrote that.'"

 That experience helped give Kelley something of a blueprint to what he'd do months later.

 
 

 INSIDE THE CASA Rios Mexican restaurant, which sits in the shadows of SoFi Stadium where Kelley played for four years with the Chargers, he was trying to finish his second film, "Leverage," without needing an extra day -- and potentially spending thousands of more dollars.

 And he was running out of time.

 "How much time do you think this scene will take?" Elena Lozonschi, an assistant director, asked Kelley.

 "About 15 minutes"

 "Can you make it 10?"

 "Sure."

 Mikaela, who had been juggling producing and breastfeeding the then 3-month-old Caleb throughout the day, handed their baby to Alex Van Dyke, Kelley's former UCLA football teammate who is in the film, and began helping by grabbing cups for a kitchen scene. Kelley ran into the back of the restaurant to help with the setup for a scene.

 In the end, Kelley got all the scenes done. The crisis was avoided, but the adrenaline rush from tense moments like that or from getting a scene to come to life exactly as he envisioned it is the closest he has gotten to the jitters he once felt from playing in the NFL.

 "I'm still kind of chasing that through filmmaking a little bit, that adrenaline rush," he said. "I feel like through filmmaking, being on set, this sort of feels again like I'm back in another playing field."

 On this playing field, Kelley has more control than he ever had as a player, when his success depended on the playcall, the quarterback and how the offensive line blocked.

 After Kelley yelled "Action!" to begin a scene, he closely watched Doss perform a scene at a table counter, but he quickly yelled, "Cut!" Kelley realized Doss' chain wasn't positioned correctly to match a previous scene and gave other directives before heading into the next scene.

 "I feel like that's why I gravitate towards this because I'm just like, I'm really in control of my destiny," he said. "I love this freedom."

 

 Kelley experienced that freedom for the first time earlier this summer while shooting "No Chaser." Kelley's goal, he said, is to make the viewer feel like they've watched something they've never seen before.

title: Can Patriots QB Drake Maye repeat MVP-caliber season in 2026?
summary: The New England quarterback is letting the Super Bowl loss motivate him in 2026, starting with the rematch at Seahawks on Wednesday.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- Navy and neon green colors filled the California air as New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye , stung by a crushing Super Bowl LX defeat , stared across the sideline in February.

 The then-23-year-old, riding the high of his team's improbable Super Bowl run, had come up short in the NFL's biggest game.

 "I think about that picture of him standing in the confetti afterwards, looking like he's trying to find Sam Darnold , and that has played in my mind -- trying to avoid that feeling ever again," Patriots quarterbacks coach Ashton Grant recalled.

 To understand Maye's approach to the upcoming 2026 season, start where the 2025 season ended. Maye was the runner-up for the NFL's Most Valuable Player award in his second NFL season after leading the league in Total QBR (77.1) and completion percentage (72%). But the young quarterback struggled in the postseason with turnovers (8) and sacks (21).

 "I've seen a determined guy who if he gets an opportunity at it again, he would like to right a lot of the things that went wrong for him," Grant said.

 

 Now, 212 days later, Maye and the Patriots visit the Seahawks to open the 2026 regular season ( Wednesday, 8:20 p.m. ET, NBC ). The burning question heading into Week 1: Will he be able to replicate the success he had in 2025?

 There are some positive signs. Maye will be playing in the same offensive system for the second straight year, something he hasn't had in the NFL. Coaches and teammates have noticed a growth in Maye as a leader and as a voice in team meetings and on the field. This offseason, he has focused on technique, like mastering the initial seconds after the snap to alleviate 2025's sack problem. And after an offseason trade by the Patriots for A.J. Brown , Maye has a true No. 1 receiver.

 "I think that people always say flush it. I think it's hard to flush a game like that in our sport," Maye said of the Super Bowl heartbreak. "At the same time, you learn from it, let it motivate you. You always wonder what it's like and I got to feel that. We didn't play our best as a team, especially myself.

 "That's something I can work on to get back, just to try to get to that same spot and be on the right side of it."

 

 Second year in McDaniels' offense 
 Shortly after players arrived for the voluntary offseason program in late April, veteran tight end Hunter Henry  was already looking forward to seeing what Maye could do in 2026.

 "This [offensive] system demands a lot on the quarterback position," Henry said. "It was kind of learning as we [went] throughout the whole [2025] season and you saw what he put out there. To have a whole offseason to build on what he did, I'm excited to see the jump."

 Maye, under the tutelage of offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels and Grant, set or tied four Patriots records in 2025. His 72% completion percentage was an all-time best for a New England QB and the sixth-highest mark in league history. He broke the team record for most games with a 100 or better passer rating with 13, which tied for the second most in NFL history. That included eight games in a row with a 100-plus passer rating, tying Tom Brady's top mark. And Maye's 91.3% completion percentage in a mid-October win over the Titans was an all-time Patriots high for a game.

 But things took a turn in the playoffs when the Patriots faced four of the NFL's best defenses (Chargers, Texans, Broncos and Seahawks). Maye struggled with turnovers and finished the postseason with a Total QBR of 40.0. Since QBR was introduced in 2006, there have been 61 instances of a quarterback making at least three starts in a single postseason, and Maye's QBR was the third lowest among that group, ahead of only Peyton Manning in his final season (2015) and Rex Grossman (2006).

 

 Maye described the difference between this season and last season as "night and day," saying it is the first time in four years he has played in the same system in consecutive seasons.

 "Naturally, [I'm] going to be more comfortable. Being in the huddle, saying the playcalls, knowing why we're running the plays, and trying to take the next level of details inside each play," he said. "I think one of the biggest things is just seeing plays that we've ran against certain defenses over and over again. I think you understand better answers, better places to go with the football, and better timing."

 McDaniels summed it up succinctly.

 "There's less explaining the foundation of what we do, and how we do it, and more trying to get really good at it this year. He knows a hell of a lot more than he did last year," he said.

 

 Finding his voice 
 Brown said he wasn't expecting what unfolded in one of his first Patriots meetings after being acquired in a trade from the Eagles on June 1.

 "Josh was speaking and [Drake] kind of cut him off. Not in a rude way, but he just kind of took over," he said. "That said so much from a young guy -- to know what he's talking about, No. 1, and to lead and be the voice of this team. When I heard that, I was like, 'Wow.'"

 Brown said it was a powerful first impression of Maye and "how much he loves his job and he studies."

 This is one part of the developmental plan that coaches have for Maye, who turned 24 on Aug. 30. They want to see him take more "ownership of the whole operation," according to Grant.

 That has manifested itself in training camp. Unlike in 2025 when Maye would convene with the coaching staff after plays, this year he instead went to teammates to tell them what he liked and didn't like on a play.

 Henry, one of Maye's closest friends on the team, has noticed the difference.

 "Just from last year to this year, he's stepping up big-time, just the leadership role," Henry said. "I feel like he's doing it within himself, though. I've been preaching that to him, 'You don't have to be anybody else man. Just be you.' He's speaking up when he needs to, able to kind of elevate guys and push guys along."

 

 Maye had always said he felt he needed to do something positive in the NFL before he could turn up the volume like that. But head coach Mike Vrabel has been among those pushing him in that area, where Maye said he has grown more comfortable but still sees room for growth.

 "I think I need to do it more -- celebrating, be louder, show my personality more," Maye said.

 Grant refers to it as the "human aspect" because Maye is still one of the team's youngest players.

 "You have to take in the realization you're a [then] 23-year-old kid and in the room with 36-year-old Morgan Moses , who's been in the league for 13 years. A.J., who's been to four Pro Bowls and named an All-Pro and Super Bowl champion. If you're not comfortable with what you're talking about, it's very hard to stand up in front of a Josh McDaniels, who's been to 10 Super Bowls, and try to overtake a meeting," Grant said.

 "The first year, we were kind of growing to that. I think Josh has done a great job with putting a battery in his bag; he charges him up and gives him the floor to say things. In our quarterback meetings, he says, 'When we go into the team meeting room, if there's something you see, something you don't like, say something. Because when you say it, it hits home [in] a different type of way.'"

 

 Addressing postseason weaknesses 
 Maye has targeted one notable area for improvement -- what happens in the immediate aftermath of him taking the snap from his new center, Jared Wilson .

 "One thing is just making the right decision in the first few seconds I have the ball in my hand," Maye said. "Knowing sometimes incompletions are the best plays, not trying to hold the ball too long, and get out of the habit of really trying to extend plays."

 Along those lines, Grant had sent Maye an ESPN article before training camp that detailed, among other things, how Broncos coach Sean Payton and his staff viewed the most effective way to defend him. Part of the scouting report noted some situations…

title: Mike Vrabel emerged from his offseason scandal. Its effects linger
summary: Mike Vrabel and the New England Patriots moved past the Dianna Russini scandal. Others are still feeling its effects.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- Mike Vrabel, the hulking former linebacker who coached his team to the Super Bowl last season, had assumed his news conference power stance: arms stretched wide to grab the lectern in front of him. It was a morning in August ahead of New England Patriots training camp practice. The head coach wore his trademark blue vest and white long-sleeved shirt.

 "What did you learn from counseling?" a reporter asked.

 Vrabel dodged the question about the scandal that rocked the NFL offseason. Instead, he turned his answer into a discussion about New England's offensive line: "I just walked into that meeting room and said, 'How do we improve? How do we improve our combination blocks?"

 He spoke for one minute and six seconds. He never mentioned the word counseling.

 

 Vrabel was the feel-good story of last NFL season as he led the Patriots from 4-13 to the Super Bowl in his first year coaching his former team.

 But after the New York Post in April published photos of him and former Athletic NFL reporter Dianna Russini together at an adults-only resort, he became a fascination beyond just sports media, crossing over into the tabloids. The attention grew so intense that Vrabel stepped away from the team to seek counseling. Vrabel's future was debated across sports media. NFL observers and personnel wondered aloud if the scrutiny on his personal life would grow into a problem on the field.

 As a new season of Super Bowl expectations begins, Vrabel's close connection to players and his track record of success have allowed him to move beyond the offseason scandal in the locker room and organization. At the same time, aftershocks continue to ripple through the league, from team front offices to the coaching ranks, in some cases changing how men who work in the league interact with women who report on it.

 ESPN spoke with league insiders, reporters, players and coaches, most of whom spoke only on the condition of anonymity, about the Patriots' offseason and how the Vrabel-Russini situation impacted the league.

 One woman who covers the NFL said that an assistant coach said he wouldn't want to be seen meeting with her because of the optics after the Vrabel scandal. Several women reporters and coaches told ESPN they are more cautious now when interacting with each other because they feel more closely watched. They worry about the league's annual scouting combine in March, an event defined by late-night intermingling between team personnel and reporters at bars that helps define coverage for fans.

 The Patriots declined to make Vrabel available for an interview and declined to comment for this story. In New England, multiple Patriots personnel and players followed Vrabel's lead, declining requests to discuss how they navigated the offseason, and those who did talk shared few details. The team offered two players -- running back Rhamondre Stevenson and safety Kevin Byard -- to speak to ESPN. "We just tried to move on as fast as we can from that," Stevenson said.

 At training camp, a group of players' and coaches' wives and girlfriends were watching practice when ESPN approached one coach's wife to discuss the strange offseason. "I love chatting," she said, "if it were any other topic."

 "We love this team, and the Pats stick together," she continued. "That's all I'll say."

 

 

 VRABEL RECEIVED A  call from a New York Post reporter on Easter Sunday regarding the photos that showed him and Russini hugging and interlocking fingers at the resort, according to a person with knowledge of the call.

 Vrabel told Page Six that the photos "show a completely innocent interaction and any suggestion otherwise is laughable." According to a person who spoke to Vrabel at the time, the head coach had wanted to issue a stronger statement that defended Russini's reporting ethics but settled on downplaying the photos.

 Russini resigned from The Athletic less than a week later. (The Athletic ultimately found that Russini's relationship with Vrabel violated its newsroom standards but that her coverage did not show a clear bias. She declined to comment for this story.) When Vrabel met reporters for the first time on April 21, he seemed chastened as he told the assembled media he'd "had some difficult conversations" with people that he cared about. He decided to miss the third day of the NFL draft to seek counseling. It was around that time that one team source noticed Vrabel was quieter than normal and not walking around the facility greeting everyone he passed as he normally would.

 The chaos continued over the following weeks as tabloids published more old photos of him together with Russini (they are both married to other people). Page Six even published photos of Vrabel in a Utah airport and reported about him and his wife having dinner. By the end of May, Vrabel held another news conference at offseason workouts and reiterated his devotion to her. "I love Jen," he told reporters.

 But if Vrabel appeared to be under siege, those inside the organization say the team had already moved on.

 

 

 ABOUT TWO WEEKS after the Post published the first photos, Patriots players and coaches gathered for a regularly scheduled meeting, their first since February's Super Bowl loss to the Seattle Seahawks. Some had followed the scandal and seen the photos.

 Vrabel spoke in the same serious tone that he used when addressing the team after a loss, according to a Patriots source. Three players in the room said Vrabel told them he was responsible for creating a distraction and bringing negative attention to the team. He said that challenges always come, but what matters is how people handle adversity when it hits, the players said.

 "He feels like he did wrong by us," Stevenson said.

 Vrabel shared no details about his relationship with Russini, nor did he explain what he'd done to cause the distraction he acknowledged, according to five people in the room. Players asked no questions, and Vrabel quickly moved on to explain the team's schedule for the day before the team broke off into smaller meetings.

 "None of the team was really even worried about specifics," Stevenson said.

 Another Patriots player reached by ESPN, who requested anonymity to speak freely, offered a different perspective: "It's difficult to explain to people outside the building how he approached it and how players took it," he said. "Of course players care about [what happened]. Vrabel is a great leader. Sometimes you have to mess up to become an even better leader."

 But simply addressing the distraction was enough accountability, four players said. "His leadership was never tied to how he lived his personal life," said the Patriots source, who noted that things would be different if Vrabel were a pastor responsible for shepherding souls and exemplifying morality.

 "Ultimately football players care about respect, they care about accountability, and they care if you can make them better," the source said. "And if you can do those things, you can be the weirdest person or you can be a stone-cold killer and they won't care."

 When players have off-the-field issues, a high-ranking executive for another NFL team told ESPN, team brass often discusses whether it should address the team. "And the answer is usually no. Players care about winning games and making money."

 Shaun Smith, a former defensive end who played with Vrabel in the NFL, suggested there could even be a newfound relatability to the coach: "Some guys are gonna be like, 'Hey, he's a dirtbag like me.' You might have some guys who want to high-five him."

 When asked about Vrabel, players and colleagues spoke glowingly about both his coaching and his humanity. He sprints to the tunnel after every game to greet each player coming off the field. He also allows players the space to prioritize their families.
